signal.title: [Bug]: OTel v2 GenAI exception events are never exported — Event body defaults to None, and the OTLP encoder drops the whole batch
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. Closest match is #32996, which reports the same *failure class* in the **v1** `OpenTelemetry._emit_semantic_logs` path. This issue is the **v2** integration (`LITELLM_OTEL_V2=true`), which has a separate emit site that none of the open PRs for #32996 (#32997, #32998) or the `gen_ai.system` PRs (#36815, #36779) touch — they all change only `litellm/integrations/opentelemetry.py`. Merging all of them leaves the v2 path broken. ### What happened? **With OTel v2 and events enabled, 100% of `gen_ai.client.operation.exception` events are silently discarded, and every log record batched alongside them goes too.** `GenAIEventRecorder.record_operation_exception` (`litellm/integrations/otel/plumbing/events.py`) builds its `Event` without a `body`: ```python self.event_logger.emit( Event( name=GenAIEvent.OPERATION_EXCEPTION, timestamp=timestamp_ns, trace_id=span_context.trace_id, ... attributes=dict(...), ) ) ``` `opentelemetry._events.Event.body` defaults to `None`. OTLP's `AnyValue` has no representation for `None`, so `_encode_value` raises while serialising the batch: ``` Exception while exporting logs. .../opentelemetry/sdk/_logs/_internal/export/__init__.py line 307, in _export_batch .../opentelemetry/exporter/otlp/proto/http/_log_exporter/__init__.py line 159, in export serialized_data = encode_logs(batch).SerializeToString() .../opentelemetry/exporter/otlp/proto/common/_internal/_log_encoder/__init__.py line 57, in _encode_log body=_encode_value(log_data.log_record.body), .../opentelemetry/exporter/otlp/proto/common/_internal/__init__.py line 90, in _encode_value raise Exception(f"Invalid type {type(value)} of value {value}") Exception: Invalid type <class 'NoneType'> of value None ``` **Why this is data loss and not log noise.** `BatchLogRecordProcessor._export_batch` catches the exception, clears the records and returns `idx` as if they were exported: ```python try: self._exporter.export(self._log_records[:idx]) except Exception: _logger.exception("Exception while exporting logs.") detach(token) for index in range(idx): self._log_records[index] = None return idx # counted as exported; never retried ``` So one unencodable record destroys the entire batch, with no crash, no retry and no signal to the operator beyond a traceback. Because `record_operation_exception` is the **only** emit site on the v2 logs signal (verified across all 38 files of `litellm/integrations/otel/` — `logger.py`'s `_emitter.emit(...)` calls are the `SpanEmitter`, i.e. spans), *every* batch on that pipeline contains only unencodable records. The result is not partial loss — the logs signal never delivers anything at all. **This is not reachable via a version bump.** Upstream OTel added a `None` branch to `_encode_value` in `opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-common` **1.43.0** (`if value is None: return PB2AnyValue()`); I bisected every release from 1.28.0 up, and 1.42.1 still raises. LiteLLM hard-pins `opentelemetry-api/-sdk/-exporter-otlp==1.28.0`, so as shipped this event can never be exported. **Why CI does not catch it:** every existing test for this event uses `InMemoryLogExporter`, which stores `LogData` objects and never encodes them. The bug only appears once something runs the OTLP encoder. ### User Flow Any proxy deployment running the v2 OTel integration with events enabled, exporting over OTLP: ``` LITELLM_OTEL_V2=true LITELLM_OTEL_INTEGRATION_ENABLE_EVENTS=true OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://<collector> OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf ``` with `litellm_settings.callbacks: ["otel"]`. Every failed LLM call then emits one unexportable event. The operator sees GenAI exception events simply never arrive at the backend, while spans and metrics arrive normally — so the pipeline looks healthy and the missing signal reads as "no errors to report". ### Proof the bug occurs **1. Standalone repro** — no litellm import, just the pinned OTel versions and the same `Event` shape. A healthy control record is emitted alongside to show the collateral loss: ```python # uv run --with opentelemetry-sdk==1.28.0 --with opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http==1.28.0 python repro.py import http.server, threading, time RECEIVED = [] class C(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def do_POST(self): RECEIVED.append(self.rfile.read(int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", 0)))) self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Length", "0"); self.end_headers() def log_message(self, *_): pass srv = http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 4318), C) threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start() from opentelemetry import _logs from opentelemetry._events import Event from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.http._log_exporter import OTLPLogExporter from opentelemetry.sdk._events import EventLoggerProvider from opentelemetry.sdk._logs import LoggerProvider from opentelemetry.sdk._logs.export import BatchLogRecordProcessor p = LoggerProvider() p.add_log_record_processor(BatchLogRecordProcessor(OTLPLogExporter(endpoint="http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/logs"))) _logs.set_logger_provider(p) ev = EventLoggerProvider(logger_provider=p).get_event_logger("litellm", "1.96.2") ev.emit(Event(name="control.healthy.event", body="i am a well-formed record")) ev.emit(Event(name="gen_ai.client.operation.exception", # litellm's event, verbatim shape attributes={"exception.type": "BadRequestError", "exception.message": "..."})) p.force_flush(10_000); time.sleep(1); srv.shutdown() print("OTLP requests delivered:", len(RECEIVED)) ``` Output — the production traceback, then: ``` OTLP requests delivered: 0 ``` The healthy control record is lost too. Re-running with `opentelemetry-*==1.43.0` gives `delivered: 1`, confirming the encoder-side fix and that 1.28.0 is where it bites. **2. Live, on a real proxy** (v1.96.2, OTLP/HTTP → collector). Two provider-side 400s produced exactly two dropped batches, ~1–5 s after each call: | event | time (UTC) | |---|---| | failing call 1 (`top_p: 5`) | 01:19:33 | | failing call 2 (`n: 99`) | 01:19:35 | | `_encode_log` batch failure | 01:19:34.5 | | `_encode_log` batch failure | 01:19:39.4 | One failed LLM call, one dropped batch — deterministic. Across three environments running v1.95.0 and v1.96.2, the backend's log table has received **0 rows in 30 days** while spans, dependencies and metrics from the same proxies flow normally. **3. Against the repo's own test suite.** Adding an encode step to the existing event test reproduces it in-tree: ```python from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.common._internal._log_encoder import encode_logs engine, _, log_exporter = _engine_with_event_recorder() engine.emit(SpanRole.LLM_CALL, _llm_call_data(SpanError(error_type="RateLimitError", message="rate limited"))) encode_logs(log_exporter.get_finished_logs()).SerializeToString() # Exception: Invalid type <class 'NoneType'> of value None ``` ### Suggested fix Set a body on the event. The exception message is the natural body for a WARN record and adds nothing the attributes don't already carry, so it is safe on every OTel version rather than dependent on a pin bump. PR to follow. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Logging / observability (OpenTelemetry v2 integration) ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.96.2 (also present on v1.95.0 and on `main` at `bd0d13566e` — `plumbing/events.py` is byte-identical across all of them)

signal.title: fix: replace Redis+in-memory temp MCP server caching with DB-backed draft servers
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - MCP OAuth sessions disappear across workers - Redis should not be required for this flow How it solves it: - Stores temporary OAuth sessions as database drafts - Uses one shared path across every worker - Excludes drafts from active server listings ## User Flow Before: a proxy admin can start MCP OAuth, but another worker cannot find the session 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/mcp/server/oauth/session with the MCP server URL and OAuth settings 2. The proxy returns 200 with a temporary `server_id` 3. Their browser sends GET https://litellm-domain/v1/mcp/server/oauth/{server_id}/authorize 4. If another worker handles the request, it returns 404 instead of redirecting to the provider After: the same OAuth session remains available from every worker 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/mcp/server/oauth/session with the MCP server URL and OAuth settings 2. The proxy returns 200 with a temporary `server_id` 3. Their browser sends GET https://litellm-domain/v1/mcp/server/oauth/{server_id}/authorize 4. Any worker returns 307 and redirects them to the provider ## Relevant issues Fixes cross-worker OAuth session lookup failures ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5514 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Before, staging at `262ed530f8`: two interleaved two-worker controls sent 80 OAuth session lookups against the live GitHub MCP upstream. 40 returned 307 and 40 returned 404. Every pinned connection saw only its worker's session After, branch at `48b78bda36` with staging parent `8841cbc10f`: 20 authorize requests across both workers returned 307, and 20 token requests reached GitHub without any 404 or 500 Drafts stayed out of active listings, discovered endpoint columns stayed null, opposite-worker finalization created one active row, TTL rejection passed on both workers, and scheduled cleanup deleted the expired draft The same revision passed 201 focused MCP tests and `make pre-commit` The A1/B/A2 method and earlier per-connection evidence are recorded in LIT-5514. Earlier summary: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/32260#issuecomment-5287046845 ## Type Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - OAuth session creation requires the existing proxy database - Successful user consent and token issuance were not exercised ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check expiry, cleanup, redaction, failures, and cross-endpoint retrieval Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/861a106f093049ca94c56249e715ac30 Requested by: @mateo-berri

signal.title: perf(spend-logs): bound retention cleanup so one run cannot saturate the database
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - One cleanup run could delete 500k rows per table, unbounded in time - A single delete batch could hold row locks indefinitely - Batch size and run length were env-only, not reachable from the dashboard - Nothing reported what the cleanup job cost the database How it solves it: - One wall-clock budget per run, shared across every table - Each batch runs under a Postgres statement_timeout and lock_timeout - Batch size, batch cap, budget and timeout are dashboard-configurable - Prometheus metrics for rows deleted, batch duration, backlog, failures, outcome ## User Flow Before: an operator who turned on spend-log retention sees the database saturate for minutes at a time whenever cleanup runs, and has no way to cap it 1. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=admin-settings, open Logging Settings, and set Maximum Spend Logs Retention Period to `30d` 2. The only other controls are two environment variables, so restarting the whole deployment is the only way to change how much work a run does 3. On the next scheduled run, cleanup deletes rows continuously for as long as it takes to reach 500,000 per table, with no way to say "spend at most N seconds on this" 4. While that runs, a single delete batch can sit holding row locks for as long as the database needs to finish it, and the request path competes with it for connections 5. https://litellm-domain/metrics carries nothing about the job, so the operator cannot see how long it ran, how much it deleted, or how much backlog is left After: the same operator caps a run from the dashboard, and can see exactly what each run cost 1. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=admin-settings, open Logging Settings, and set Maximum Spend Logs Retention Period to `30d` 2. On the same page they set Spend Logs Cleanup Run Budget to `30s` and Spend Logs Cleanup Batch Timeout to `10s`, then save 3. On the next scheduled run, cleanup stops after 30 seconds and leaves the rest of the backlog for the following run, which picks up where it left off 4. A batch that would otherwise block is cancelled by the database at 10 seconds, so it cannot hold row locks or a pooled connection past that 5. https://litellm-domain/metrics now reports `litellm_spend_log_cleanup_rows_deleted_total`, `litellm_spend_log_cleanup_batch_duration_seconds`, `litellm_spend_log_cleanup_rows_remaining`, `litellm_spend_log_cleanup_batch_failures_total` and `litellm_spend_log_cleanup_runs_total`, the last labelled by why the run ended ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5439 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [ ] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Sections 1 to 4 are against a real Postgres 16 holding 2,000,000 spend-log rows and 2,000,000 tool-index rows, of which 1,000,006 are expired at a 30 day cutoff. Their before runs are at `bea31871fc` (the merge base at the time), after runs at `72a1d55625`. Section 5 was captured for the propagation fix, arms `25466e6082` against `c8789cecca`. Section 6 was captured for the budget fix, arms `c8789cecca` against `b428c3f3dc`. The current head `e5227dc467` adds the partition-DDL bound and the YAML-fallback fix on top. None of that can move the earlier numbers: sections 1 to 4 exercise bounds that were already in force, section 5 ran with the default 300s run budget against a 7s batch timeout so clamping to the budget still leaves it at 7s, and section 6 ran with partitioning disabled, which is the shipped default ### Setup ``` $ docker run -d --name litfix-5439-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=litellm -e POSTGRES_USER=litellm \ -e POSTGRES_DB=litellm -p 5878:5432 postgres:16 $ prisma db push --schema litellm/proxy/schema.prisma $ docker exec -i litfix-5439-pg psql -U litellm -d litellm -f - < seed.sql INSERT 0 2000000 INSERT 0 2000000 total | expired ---------+--------- 2000000 | 1000006 ``` ### 1. A run is unbounded in time before, and respects its budget after Before, at `bea31871fc`. Each run simply continues until it hits the 500,000 row cap: ``` $ grep -c "SET LOCAL statement_timeout" litellm/proxy/db/db_transaction_queue/spend_log_cleanup.py 0 $ PYTHONPATH=<base worktree> python proof.py budget litellm loaded from: .../lit5439-base/litellm settings: {'maximum_spend_logs_retention_period': '30d'} run 1: deleted 500958 spend-log rows in 109.3s (expired remaining: 499053) run 2: deleted 499011 spend-log rows in 109.7s (expired remaining: 42) ``` After, at `72a1d55625`, with `maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_run_budget: 30s`. Both runs stop on the budget and the backlog drains across runs: ``` $ grep -c "SET LOCAL statement_timeout" litellm/proxy/db/db_transaction_queue/spend_log_cleanup.py 1 $ PYTHONPATH=<branch worktree> python proof.py budget litellm loaded from: .../tidy-finding-starfish/litellm settings: {'maximum_spend_logs_retention_period': '30d', 'maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_run_budget': '30s'} run 1: deleted 254988 spend-log rows in 30.2s (expired remaining: 745021) run 2: deleted 255989 spend-log rows in 30.1s (expired remaining: 489032) ``` ### 2. A slow batch holds locks without bound before, and is cancelled after To make a batch outlive any client patience on demand, each deleted row sleeps 0.5s in a `BEFORE DELETE` trigger, so a 20 row batch needs about 10s of server work. Both arms use `SPEND_LOG_CLEANUP_BATCH_SIZE=20` and `SPEND_LOG_RUN_LOOPS=1`, which both branches honour, so the only difference between them is the per-batch timeout this PR adds. Each leg asserts no transaction was already open before it started, so a leftover from the previous leg cannot be attributed to it. The observable is what the database is holding, polled from `pg_stat_activity`, not what the client reports. Before, at `bea31871fc`. The hold is set purely by how much work the batch is, with nothing capping it: ``` pre-flight: no pre-existing open transactions [base] open transaction on LiteLLM_SpendLogs held 1.0s state=active ... [base] open transaction on LiteLLM_SpendLogs held 10.0s state=active batch attempt returned after 20.6s; longest transaction the DB held: 10.0s ``` After, at `72a1d55625`, with `maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_batch_timeout: 3s`. Postgres cancels the statement at the configured bound: ``` pre-flight: no pre-existing open transactions [fixed] open transaction on LiteLLM_SpendLogs held 1.0s state=active [fixed] open transaction on LiteLLM_SpendLogs held 2.0s state=active [fixed] open transaction on LiteLLM_SpendLogs held 2.5s state=active batch attempt returned after 10.2s; longest transaction the DB held: 2.5s prisma.errors.RawQueryError: ERROR: canceling statement due to statement timeout Aborting LiteLLM_SpendLogs cleanup after 3 consecutive batch failures; total deleted before abort: 0 ``` That last line is the intended behaviour when the timeout is set below what one batch legitimately needs: the job gives up loudly and records the failures, rather than hanging. At the shipped defaults the margin is large, since a 1000 row batch measures at 1.8ms against this table. ### 3. Why the batch plan itself is not the problem Worth stating because it redirects tuning away from the delete statement. The per-batch plan is an index scan, not a table scan, so the cost of a large backlog is WAL volume and the autovacuum load from dead tuples rather than the plan: ``` Delete on "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" (actual time=1.720..1.721 rows=0 loops=1) -> Nested Loop (actual time=0.521..1.441 rows=1000 loops=1) -> HashAggregate (actual time=0.515..0.623 rows=1000 loops=1) -> Limit (actual time=0.037..0.269 rows=1000 loops=1) -> Index Scan using "LiteLLM_SpendLogs_startTime_idx" ... Execution Time: 1.831 ms ``` One unbounded run leaves roughly a million dead tuples across the two tables and triggers repeated autovacuum on both: ``` relname | n_live_tup | n_dead_tup | n_tup_del | autovacuum_count ---------------------------+------------+------------+-----------+------------------ LiteLLM_SpendLogToolIndex | 1495000 | 94000 | 501000 | 2 LiteLLM_SpendLogs | 1500227 | 0 | 502000 | 2 ``` The poll samples once a second, so it last observed the transaction at 2.5s before Postgres cancelled it at the 3s bound; the base leg above was still holding at 10.0s with nothing to cancel it. ### 5. The dashboard bounds reach the running job Cursor Bugbot found that the four new knobs were read once when `SpendLogCleanup` was constructed and never propagated into the in-memory `general_settings` at all, so the controls section 4 shows the wire contract for did nothing to the next run. It was right, and both halves were real. The observable is what the database is told, not what the API returns: every batch this job issues opens with `SET LOCAL statement_timeout`, so the configured per-batch bound appears verbatim in the Postgres statement log. Both arms run one proxy against a real Postgres with `log_statement=all`, seeded with 6,000 expired rows, on a 20 second cleanup interval, and push the same `/config/update` the dashboard sends. Neither arm restarts. Before, at `25466e6082`. The update is accepted and the value is stored, and the job never sees it: ``` $ curl -X POST localhost:4079/config/update -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ -d '{"general_settings": {"maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_batch_timeout": "7s", "maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_batch_size": 250}}' config_update=200 {"message":"Config updated successfully"} $ psql -c "SELECT param_value->>'maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_batch_timeout', param_value->>'maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_batch_size' FROM \"LiteLLM_Config\" WHERE param_name='general_settings';" 7s | 250 $ docker logs <pg> | grep -oE 'SET LOCAL statement_timeout = [0-9]+' | sort | uniq -c 40 SET LOCAL statement_timeout = 30000 ``` Forty statements across every tick that followed the update, all still at the 30 second default. After, on the current head. Same rig, same request, and the ticks before the update are the control: ``` $ docker logs <pg> | grep -E '^2026.*SET LOCAL statement_timeout' | ... | uniq -c 14 18:30 30000 <- control, shipped defaults 12 18:31 30000 <- control 36 18:32 7000 <- first tick after /config/update 8 18:33 7000 $ grep -c "SpendLogCleanup initialized" proxy.log 1 ``` That last line is what rules out the boring explanation: the class logs its bounds once per construction, so a single occurrence means the same long-lived instance changed its own bounds with no restart and no rebuild of the job. The statement count moving from 12 to 36 against an identically re-seeded 6,000 rows is the batch size knob landing at the same moment, 1000 down to 250. ### 6. The run budget is a hard bound Bugbot's second round pointed out that the budget was advisory, and it was right about the mechanism. The budget is checked between statements, and Postgres has no "stop at time T", only a per-statement duration. So a batch issued just under the deadline still got the full batch timeout, and every table exits through a code path that then issued an outstanding-rows probe, including the tables a spent run never started. With three tables those stack. Every statement is now issued with its timeout clamped to the budget that is left, and no statement is issued at all once the budget is spent. To make a batch outlive any budget on demand, each deleted row sleeps 0.5s in a `BEFORE DELETE` trigger, so a 40 row batch needs about 20s of server work against a 5s budget. Both arms assert the trigger is installed before they start, since a run that quietly finished at normal speed would look like a pass. Before, at `c8789cecca`: ``` pre-flight: slow-delete trigger installed (0.5s per row, batch_size=40) settings: run_budget=5.0s batch_timeout=30.0s batch_size=40 run budget: 5.0s run took: 20.8s overrun: +15.8s (4.2x the budget) ``` After, on the current head: ``` pre-flight: slow-delete trigger installed (0.5s per row, batch_size=40) settings: run_budget=5.0s batch_timeout=30.0s batch_size=40 run budget: 5.0s run took: 5.0s overrun: +0.0s (1.0x the budget) ``` That left partition maintenance as the one unbounded exception, and it is now closed too. `ensure_partitions` and `drop_partitions_older_than` issued bare `CREATE TABLE` and `DROP TABLE` in loops with no timeout of any kind, and a DROP takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, so it could queue behind a long-running reader for as long as that reader lived. Every statement this path issues now carries a timeout, the two catalog lookups included, and the DDL also carries a `lock_timeout`, so a partition this run cannot get is left for the next one. To be precise about which bound does the work: `statement_timeout` already covers time spent waiting for a lock, so it alone would bound this; `lock_timeout` is set alongside it to mirror the delete path and to fail fast on contention specifically. The defect was that neither was set at all. The bound is injected as a callable rather than passed as a number, which is the part that makes the LOOPS bounded rather than just the individual statements. These loops issue one statement per partition, so a number read once at entry would let every one of them run for the budget that was left before the first, which is no bound on the loop at all. It is re-read before each statement, and a run whose budget is gone stops instead of issuing work it cannot pay for. So no statement this job issues can outlast the run budget. ### 7. Partition maintenance, driven live Sections 1 to 6 all ran with `use_spend_logs_partitioning` off, which is the shipped default, so none of them exercised the DDL path at all. Its unit tests stub `db.tx()`, which cannot tell you whether prisma's interactive transaction really carries `CREATE TABLE` and `DROP TABLE`. Against a real range-partitioned table it does, and the catalog is read back rather than the return value trusted: ``` pre-flight: LiteLLM_SpendLogs is range-partitioned before: ['LiteLLM_SpendLogs_p20250101'] ensure_partitions -> 3 ensured: ['..._p20260813', '..._p20260814', '..._p20260815'] after create: ['..._p20250101', '..._p20260813', '..._p20260814', '..._p20260815'] all 3 partitions really exist in the catalog drop_partitions_older_than -> dropped: ['LiteLLM_SpendLogs_p20250101'] after drop: ['..._p20260813', '..._p20260814', '..._p20260815'] the expired partition is really gone from the catalog ``` And the Postgres statement log shows the bounds arriving ahead of every one of them: ``` SET LOCAL statement_timeout = 7000 SET LOCAL lock_timeout = 7000 CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "LiteLLM_SpendLogs_p20260813" PARTITION OF "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" ... ``` The discriminating case is a DROP that cannot get its lock. A second session holds ACCESS SHARE on the partition for 25 seconds while the drop runs with a 3 second bound: ``` pre-flight: a reader holds ACCESS SHARE on the partition for 25s lock_timeout given: 3.0s reader holds for: 25s drop attempt took: 3.0s dropped: [] Failed to drop spend-log partition LiteLLM_SpendLogs_p20250101: ERROR: canceling statement due to statement timeout PASS: the drop gave up after ~3.0s instead of waiting 25s for the reader ``` Before this change that attempt had no timeout of any kind and would have waited out the reader, however long it lived. The partition is simply left in place and the next run retries it, which is the warning line above. ### 4. Admin UI The four new controls sit next to the existing retention period on Logging Settings. Rather than a screenshot of the form, here is the wire contract behind it, driven against a live proxy through the exact endpoints that page calls. `/config/list` serves all four with their types, `/config/update` accepts them and they read back, and `/config/field/delete` (what a blank field triggers on save) clears one while leaving its siblings intact: ``` === 1. the four knobs are served by /config/list, unset === maximum_spend_logs_retention_period String '30d' maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_batch_size Integer None maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_max_batches Integer None maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_run_budget String None maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_batch_timeout String None === 2. set them via /config/update, exactly as the dashboard does === HTTP 200 === 3. read back === maximum_spend_logs_retention_period String '30d' maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_batch_size Integer 2000 maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_max_batches Integer 250 maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_run_budget String '90s' maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_batch_timeout String '10s' === 4. clear one via /config/field/delete, the path a blank field takes === HTTP 200 maximum_spend_logs_retention_period String '30d' maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_batch_size Integer 2000 maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_max_batches Integer 250 maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_run_budget String None maximum_spend_logs_cleanup_batch_timeout String '10s' ``` That sequential clear is load-bearing rather than cosmetic: `/config/field/delete` reads the whole stored `general_settings` object, pops one key and writes the object back, so the form issues those clears one at a time. In parallel the last write wins and restores the fields the earlier ones just cleared. The form itself is covered by 19 unit tests, including that a blank field is absent from the save payload rather than present-and-empty, that clears never overlap, and that a failed clear reports an error instead of success. ### Tests Every new behaviour is pinned by a mutation check: 12 mutants, each reverting one added behaviour separately, all killed. The `math.isfinite` guard an earlier revision carried was found to be unreachable (the duration parser already rejects `inf`, `nan` and `1e400`) and was removed rather than left as untested dead code. ## Review notes **Fourth round: Greptile 4/5 and a Bugbot Medium, both on the same gap, both real and both fixed.** **Catalog queries stayed outside the budget (Greptile).** Correct. Bounding the DDL left `is_partitioned` and `_list_partitions` as statements this job issues with no bound at all, while the docstring had just started claiming that no statement could outlast the budget. Both now run under the same clamped timeout **Partition DDL budget not re-clamped (Bugbot).** Correct, and the sharper of the two. The bound was computed once before partition maintenance and reused for every CREATE and DROP, so a loop over N partitions could issue N statements each bounded by the budget that was left before the first of them. That is a bound on each statement and not on the loop. The bound is now injected as a callable that is re-read before every statement, and returns None once the budget is spent so the loop stops rather than issuing doomed work. Driven against real Postgres: with a spent budget, `is_partitioned`, `ensure_partitions` and `drop_partitions_older_than` issue no statement at all **Third Bugbot round, one finding, real and fixed.** **Cleared YAML override stayed in memory (Medium).** Correct, and it was a defect in the propagation fix from the round before. When a bound is declared in config.yaml AND then overridden from the dashboard, clearing it removed the DB key, but the guard that protects a YAML-declared bound from being treated as a clear meant memory kept the DELETED override until restart. The operator cleared the field and the value they removed stayed in force. The reload now tracks the YAML VALUES rather than only which keys YAML set, so a clear falls back to the YAML value, or to the shipped default when YAML declared nothing. That also made the branch simpler than what it replaced **Partition maintenance was the last unbounded path, closed in the same push.** Not filed by a bot; it came out of re-reading the budget claim after the round above. `ensure_partitions` and `drop_partitions_older_than` issued their DDL with no timeout at all, so a DROP could queue behind a long-running reader indefinitely and the run budget could not cut it short. Both now carry `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout`. Typing the three `prisma_client` parameters that this touched also took the module from 25 basedpyright errors to 16 **Second Bugbot round, both findings real and both fixed.** **Run budget was advisory, not enforced (Medium).** Correct, and my own docstring was the inaccurate part: it claimed a run could overrun by at most one batch timeout, when the true worst case was one in-flight batch plus one probe per table. Statement timeouts are now clamped to the remaining budget and no statement is issued once the budget is spent, which is what section 6 measures. A batch cancelled by its own clamp is classified as budget exhaustion rather than a database fault, so it neither inflates the batch-failure metric nor walks a budget-exhausted run toward the abort threshold. The cost, stated plainly: the outstanding-rows gauge keeps its previous value for a table whose run ended on the budget, since refreshing it would mean one more statement past the bound **Clears blocked the first save (High).** Correct, and it was a regression from the previous round's fix. Blanking an optional field issues `/config/field/delete`, that endpoint answers 400 when no `general_settings` row exists at all, and the previous round had made a failed clear abort the save. A fresh deployment has no such row, confirmed against a live proxy, so the very first save on a new proxy reported an error and persisted nothing. The form now only clears a field that actually has a stored value, so there is nothing to fail. A genuine clear failure still aborts and still reports, which is the behaviour the earlier round added **The approval on this PR is stale.** It was given against `25466e6082`. Everything after that commit is the Bugbot round below, which changes runtime behaviour rather than tests, so this wants a fresh look before it merges **Dashboard cleanup knobs never applied (Cursor Bugbot, High).** Correct on both halves, and together they made the feature inert. `_update_general_settings` is an allowlist, and the four new keys were not on it, so a `/config/update` reached the database and stopped there. Separately, the scheduler holds one long-lived `SpendLogCleanup` whose bounds were parsed in `__init__`, so even once the keys arrived the running job kept the values it started with. The pre-existing `maximum_spend_logs_retention_period` has neither problem, since it is on the allowlist and is re-read every run, and that asymmetry was the bug. The bounds are now re-read at the top of each run, exactly as the retention period already was, and the reload copies them across. Clearing one from the dashboard restores its default; a bound set in config.yaml is left alone, since it never appears in the database object and treating its absence as a clear would discard the deployed config on every reload. Section 5 above is the live before and after. Four mutants, one per added behaviour, all killed: dropping the per-run re-read, dropping the propagation, clearing without the YAML guard, and never clearing Greptile's first pass raised three P1s against `68d64b1675` and scored it 2/5. All three were real and all three are fixed; none were rebutted. The re-review came back 5/5, and `25466e6082` was later re-reviewed at 5/5 in its own right after a tests-only change: a parametrized test pinning run-outcome precedence across both orderings of every pair, which raised local coverage of the cleanup module from 98% to 99% and kills two further mutants. Both of those scores predate the Bugbot round above, so neither is a verdict on the current head **Run budget excluded some database work.** Correct. The budget bounded the delete loop but not the outstanding-rows probe that follows it, nor partition maintenance. The probe now runs inside a transaction carrying the same `statement_timeout` the delete batches use, so no statement this job issues is unbounded. Partition maintenance is different in kind: dropping a partition is DDL holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and cannot be cut short once started, so it is now only STARTED while budget remains, and a run that is already over skips it for the next tick to pick up. The class docstring states the resulting honest bound: a run can overrun its budget by at most one batch timeout. **Parallel deletes lost cleared settings.** Correct, and worse than it reads. `/config/field/delete` is a full-object read-modify-write: it reads the whole stored `general_settings`, pops one key, and writes the whole object back. Five of those in flight at once is last-writer-wins, so clearing five fields could leave four still set while the form reported success. They now run strictly one at a time. **Deletion failures reported success.** Correct. The promise resolved on `onSettled` and only logged to the console, so a failed clear still showed "updated successfully" while the old value stayed in force. A failed clear now surfaces through the notification manager and suppresses the success path. Every fix is pinned by a mutation check rather than only by a passing test: restoring `Promise.all` fails exactly the new concurrency test, restoring the swallow fails exactly the new failure-reporting test, removing the probe's timeout fails the probe test, and ignoring the spent budget before partition DDL fails the partition test. Eighteen mutants across this PR, all killed. ## Type 🆕 New Feature 🚄 Infrastructure ## Caveats (if any) - Batch cap now means exactly N statements, previously N+1 - No statement this job issues can outlast the run budget, partition DDL included - A partition whose lock is held by a long-running reader is left for the next run - The outstanding-rows gauge is not refreshed for a table whose run ended on the budget - Docs land separately in BerriAI/litellm-docs#866, which must merge first - `documentation` and `code-quality` stay red until that docs PR merges ## QA runbook ### Final Attestation - [ ] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > <sup>[Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) is generating a summary for commit 25466e6082440c64170b08625fcffdfc530fea96. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: feat(azure/realtime): support Azure AD (Entra ID) auth for realtime websocket
signal.text: ## Title feat(azure/realtime): support Azure AD (Entra ID) auth for realtime websocket ## Relevant issues Fixes #34654 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have Added testing in the [`tests/litellm/`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/tree/main/tests/litellm) directory, **Adding at least 1 test is a hard requirement** - [see details](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/extras/contributing_code) - [x] I have added a screenshot of my new test passing locally - [x] My PR passes all unit tests on `make test-unit` - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible, it only solves 1 specific problem ## Type 🆕 New Feature 🐛 Bug Fix ## Changes The Azure OpenAI **realtime** websocket path only ever sent an `api-key` header, so Azure deployments authenticated with **Azure AD / Entra ID** (managed identity, service principal, OIDC, …) and **no static API key** could not connect. This blocks real deployments such as `gpt-realtime-whisper` on Azure AI Foundry secured with Entra ID only. This PR wires the realtime path into the existing `get_azure_ad_token` helper, mirroring the canonical precedence already used by non-realtime Azure flows (`BaseAzureLLM._base_validate_azure_environment`). **`litellm/realtime_api/main.py`** - In the `azure` branch of `_arealtime`, resolve the token via `get_azure_ad_token(litellm_params)` (only when an explicit token wasn't passed) instead of hard-coding `azure_ad_token=None`, and forward it to `async_realtime`. - In `_realtime_health_check`, when no `api-key` is present for an Azure deployment, authenticate the handshake with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Non-Azure providers keep their existing behavior. **`litellm/llms/azure/realtime/handler.py`** - `AzureOpenAIRealtime.async_realtime` now selects a **single** auth header: prefer `api-key`, fall back to `Authorization: Bearer <azure_ad_token>`, never both. Matches `_base_validate_azure_environment` precedence. **Scope isolation:** this change only adds Azure AD auth for the realtime websocket (+ its health check). No other providers or behaviors are touched; `api-key` deployments are unaffected. ## Testing Added mocked tests in `tests/test_litellm/llms/azure/realtime/test_azure_realtime_handler.py`: - `test_async_realtime_uses_api_key_header_when_present` — api-key precedence; no `Authorization` sent even if a token is also present. - `test_async_realtime_uses_bearer_token_when_no_api_key` — falls back to `Authorization: Bearer`, no `api-key` sent. - `test_arealtime_resolves_and_forwards_azure_ad_token` — `_arealtime` resolves via `get_azure_ad_token` and forwards it (guards against regressing to hard-coded `None`). - `test_realtime_health_check_uses_bearer_token_for_azure` — AAD-only health check uses the bearer header. ``` $ uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/llms/azure/realtime/test_azure_realtime_handler.py -q ........................... [100%] 27 passed in 0.34s ``` Also verified `ruff format --check` clean and modules import without circular-import regressions.

signal.title: fix(batches): stop uncostable batches from starving the cost poll page
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Uncostable batches held poll slots forever - Once they filled the page, newer batches went uncosted - Terminal rows escaped the staleness sweep entirely How it solves it: - Retire rows with no model id in their unified id - Retire rows the provider 404s as gone - Sweep completed rows never costed past the staleness cutoff ## User Flow Before: a customer submitting daily batches sees new batches stop showing any spend, with no error anywhere 1. Over time some of their batches become uncostable, either because the id the gateway handed back carries no routable model or because the provider has since dropped its record of the batch 2. Once enough of those pile up, they submit a fresh batch: POST https://litellm-domain/v1/batches with an `input_file_id` and get back `202` with a scrambled batch id and `"status": "validating"` 3. They fire and forget, since the gateway's background cost job has always billed completed batches on its own (polling GET https://litellm-domain/v1/batches/{id} after completion is the one escape hatch, because retrieving a completed batch bills it on the spot) 4. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs and there is no spend row for that batch, and none appears an hour later, or the next day 5. The only way out is to go into the database by hand and mark the dead batches processed After: the dead batches drop out on their own and the fresh batch gets costed like it always did 1. Same starting point, with the same pile of uncostable batches 2. They submit the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/batches and get the same `202` with `"status": "validating"` 3. They fire and forget just the same 4. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs shows that batch at real non-zero spend within the first poll cycle after it completes 5. No manual database surgery, and the dead batches stay out of the way for good ## Relevant issues Fixes #36640 ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5462 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Full before and after pair at this PR's final head `3b09484344`, before at the exact merge base `5f2986a1f3` (port 30397), after at the head (port 47613). Each leg ran in its own fresh worktree with its own venv and a fresh database, a live proxy against the real OpenAI batch API, and `PROXY_BATCH_POLLING_INTERVAL=60` with `MAX_OBJECTS_PER_POLL_CYCLE=2` so two dead rows are enough to fill the poll page. The model id is pinned so the seeded 404 row resolves to a live deployment ```yaml model_list: - model_name: gpt-4o-mini litellm_params: model: openai/gpt-4o-mini api_key: os.environ/OPENAI_API_KEY model_info: id: qa-fixed-gpt4omini mode: batch general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL litellm_settings: require_managed_files: true ``` Both legs ran the identical script. Seed two dead rows 10 and 9 days old at terminal status `complete` with `batch_processed=false`: one whose unified id decodes to `litellm_proxy;llm_batch_id:poison-no-model` (no model id), one encoding `model_id:qa-fixed-gpt4omini;llm_batch_id:batch_deadbeef0000000000000000000000` (404 at OpenAI). Submit a real batch, fire and forget. Once OpenAI reports it complete, seed two more identical dead rows minutes old, too young for the 7 day sweep, and submit a second real batch. The batches are never retrieved through the proxy, because retrieval bills inline on both versions and would mask the background job; completion is confirmed against the provider directly ```bash printf '%s\n' '{"custom_id":"r1","method":"POST","url":"/v1/chat/completions","body":{"model":"gpt-4o-mini","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"say hi in 3 words"}],"max_tokens":20}}' > batch_input.jsonl FID=$(curl -s http://localhost:<port>/v1/files -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" \ -F purpose="batch" -F target_model_names="gpt-4o-mini" \ -F file="@batch_input.jsonl;type=application/jsonl" | jq -r .id) BID=$(curl -s http://localhost:<port>/v1/batches -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d "{\"input_file_id\":\"$FID\",\"endpoint\":\"/v1/chat/completions\",\"completion_window\":\"24h\"}" | jq -r .id) PROVIDER_BID=$(python3 -c "import base64,sys;s=sys.argv[1];print(next(p.split(':',1)[1] for p in base64.urlsafe_b64decode(s+'='*(-len(s)%4)).decode().split(';') if p.startswith('llm_batch_id:')))" "$BID") curl -s "https://api.openai.com/v1/batches/$PROVIDER_BID" -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" | jq '{id,status,completed_at}' curl -s "http://localhost:<port>/spend/logs" -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" | jq 'sort_by(.startTime) | map({call_type, spend, total_tokens, startTime})' ``` ### Before, merge base `5f2986a1f3` Both creates returned `202` with a unified id and `"status": "validating"`, and OpenAI finished each batch within about a minute of submission ``` batch 1: batch_6a7e6ba3c1c8819092dcb86945621c09 completed_at 2026-08-14T01:14:15Z batch 2: batch_6a7e6c25ac9081908a22a39bf31247f8 completed_at 2026-08-14T01:16:00Z ``` The final /spend/logs read at 01:37:36Z, about 20 poll cycles after batch 1 completed and 19 after batch 2, still holds nothing but the four $0 create rows. Neither batch is ever costed, the starvation in one screen ``` [ { "call_type": "acreate_file", "spend": 0.0, "total_tokens": 0, "startTime": "2026-08-14T01:13:06.755000Z" }, { "call_type": "acreate_batch", "spend": 0.0, "total_tokens": 0, "startTime": "2026-08-14T01:13:07.606000Z" }, { "call_type": "acreate_file", "spend": 0.0, "total_tokens": 0, "startTime": "2026-08-14T01:15:17.130000Z" }, { "call_type": "acreate_batch", "spend": 0.0, "total_tokens": 0, "startTime": "2026-08-14T01:15:17.532000Z" } ] ``` ### After, head `3b09484344` Same creates, same fire and forget ``` batch 1: batch_6a7e6be9fbfc8190b855df266788f734 completed_at 2026-08-14T01:16:14Z batch 2: batch_6a7e6c88d6b08190ac0d58326e39bec0 completed_at 2026-08-14T01:17:50Z ``` The /spend/logs read at 01:23:19Z shows both batches costed by the background job with zero client retrievals at any point. Batch 1's spend row lands 29 seconds after provider completion, within one 60s cycle. Batch 2's lands 97 seconds after: the first post-completion cycle's two slots went to the fresh poison rows, retired on sight, and the very next cycle costed the batch ``` [ { "call_type": "acreate_file", "spend": 0.0, "total_tokens": 0, "startTime": "2026-08-14T01:14:16.753000Z" }, { "call_type": "acreate_batch", "spend": 0.0, "total_tokens": 0, "startTime": "2026-08-14T01:14:17.704000Z" }, { "call_type": "aretrieve_batch", "spend": 0.000002475, "total_tokens": 18, "startTime": "2026-08-14T01:16:43.388000Z" }, { "call_type": "acreate_file", "spend": 0.0, "total_tokens": 0, "startTime": "2026-08-14T01:16:56.255000Z" }, { "call_type": "acreate_batch", "spend": 0.0, "total_tokens": 0, "startTime": "2026-08-14T01:16:56.688000Z" }, { "call_type": "aretrieve_batch", "spend": 0.000002475, "total_tokens": 18, "startTime": "2026-08-14T01:19:27.324000Z" } ] ``` Kept from the earlier live run at `c11ebbed27`: screenshots and a screen recording of the Admin UI logs page showing the costed batch under the `LiteLLM Proxy/CheckBatchCost` user agent are in [this Slack thread](https://berriaillm.slack.com/archives/C09MMPFRN7M/p1786543889731829?thread_ts=1786543889.731829&cid=C09MMPFRN7M) and in a comment below. That run also probed the other direction: a row pointed at an unreachable deployment kept retrying across 9 cycles and a raw non-base64 unified id was never retired, so only provably dead rows are dropped. A 404 alone is still not trusted, since retirement needs the error to name the batch id and the batch's own deployment to still be in the router, so a renamed Azure deployment or a fallback that never saw the batch keeps retrying Observations from this run: - Fresh retirements delayed batch 2's costing one cycle (this PR, bounded) - Pre-fix, dead 404 rows re-hit OpenAI every cycle (this PR removes) ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Transient failures still retry, bounded only by the staleness cutoff - Old schemas without `batch_processed` retire by status instead - Retrieving a completed batch already billed it inline, on both versions Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/d5c8c2d2e44f4033a4500e9cf415b306 Requested by: @mateo-berri ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Changes batch spend attribution and when rows stop being polled; incorrect retirement could drop legitimate spend, though 404 handling is narrowed and heavily tested. > > **Overview** > Fixes **LIT-5462**: uncostable managed batch rows could fill every slot in the paginated `CheckBatchCost` poll (`MAX_OBJECTS_PER_POLL_CYCLE`), so newer batches never got costed or showed spend. > > **During each poll**, rows that can never succeed are **retired** via `_retire_job` (sets `batch_processed=True`, or `stale_expired` on schemas without that column): unified IDs that decode but have **no `model_id`**, and provider **404s that explicitly name the batch** when the batch’s deployment is still on the router. Misrouted 404s (missing deployment, wrong Azure deployment name, transient errors) are **not** retired so spend can still be recovered after config fixes. > > **Stale cleanup** adds a second sweep for old **`complete`/`completed`** rows still at `batch_processed=False`, since the existing non-terminal staleness pass never touched them. Terminal status lists are centralized in **`TERMINAL_MANAGED_OBJECT_STATUSES`**. > > Regression coverage lives in **`TestPollPageStarvation`** in the proxy unit tests. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 3b09484344defaf64a475f97f9b5ad0de35bce8b. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: [Bug]: CheckBatchCost starves on rows it can never route, and latches its schema probe off on unrelated errors
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? `CheckBatchCost` reconciles batch spend by reading a fixed-size page of unprocessed managed objects ordered oldest-first: ```python jobs = await self.prisma_client.db.litellm_managedobjecttable.find_many( where={"file_purpose": "batch", "batch_processed": False, "status": {"not_in": ["failed", "expired", "cancelled", "stale_expired"]}}, take=MAX_OBJECTS_PER_POLL_CYCLE, order={"created_at": "asc"}, ) ``` Any row that cannot be costed is `continue`d without being marked, so it is still `batch_processed = false` on the next cycle and is selected again. Because the ordering is `created_at ASC` and the page size is fixed, a row that can *never* be costed permanently occupies a slot. Enough such rows fill the page, and no newer batch is ever reached. Reconciliation is the only path to spend for any batch the client does not itself poll to completion. `_update_batch_object_status` marks `batch_processed = True` on the retrieve path and comments that "CheckBatchCost acts as a safety net for the rare case where the callback fails" — so for a fire-and-forget batch (submit, come back tomorrow for the output file) the safety net is the *only* net, and a starved queue means that spend is never recorded at all. In our environment this ran undetected for roughly 11 months: **no batch had ever been marked reconciled — 0 of 1,738 rows.** Nothing surfaces this. Batch creation, retrieval and output download all keep returning 200, so a user sees healthy batches; only the spend total is silently wrong. There is no error, no metric that crosses a threshold, and no log line that says reconciliation has stopped — just the same batch ids being picked up again every cycle. Two independent defects each produce this stall. They are one issue because the fix for each is the same judgement — *is this failure permanent or transient?* — and fixing only one leaves the queue just as stallable. **1. A batch that can never be routed is retried forever.** Reconciliation has to map a stored batch back to a model group to price it. That mapping can fail for reasons that are permanent properties of the stored batch — an id that carries no resolvable model — and for reasons that are purely configuration and would resolve on a config change. Both are treated identically: retried next cycle. The permanent ones therefore occupy the page forever. The distinction matters in both directions, and getting it wrong is expensive either way. Retiring too eagerly writes off real spend irreversibly; retiring nothing at all stalls the queue. Concretely, of the ways the mapping can fail, only one is immutable: | cause of routing failure | permanent? | correct action | |---|---|---| | a proxy-generated batch id that decodes without any model id | yes — no config change can fix it | retire once, unbilled | | unmanaged-batch tracking is off, so a legacy id is skipped | no — enabling it makes these billable | keep retrying | | unmanaged tracking on, but no cloud-storage model in the input file id | no | keep retrying | | model group resolved, but no such deployment in the router now | no — restoring the group fixes it | keep retrying | **2. A batch whose provider-side record is gone is retried forever.** Retrieval errors are caught with a bare handler that cannot distinguish permanent from transient: ```python except Exception as e: verbose_proxy_logger.info(f"Skipping job {job.unified_object_id} because of error querying ...: {e}") if prom_logger: prom_logger.record_check_batch_cost_error("provider_retrieval_error") continue ``` A 404 (`batch_not_found`) is provably permanent: providers expire batch records, and no retry will bring one back. Treating it like a 5xx makes it the new page head forever. In our environment this was 860 rows, and it became the blocker as soon as defect 1 was cleared. **Expected:** a failure that is provably permanent — an id that can never resolve a model, a provider 404 — retires the row once so it stops occupying the queue, while every configuration-dependent or transient failure keeps retrying. ### User Flow ### User Flow **Before a fix: a team lead who runs nightly batch jobs sees $0.00 spend for every batch, forever, because one old batch sits at the head of the reconciliation queue and never clears** 1. They submit a batch: `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/files` with `purpose=batch`, `target_model_names`, and a JSONL body, which returns `200` and a scrambled gateway file id (not the provider's own `file-abc123` shape) 2. They create the batch: `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/batches` with that file id, `endpoint=/v1/chat/completions`, `completion_window=24h` — returns `200` with a scrambled batch id 3. The batch is left to run overnight; nothing polls it. The provider completes it and bills for it 4. Next morning they download the results: `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/files/{output_file_id}/content` returns `200` with the real completions. **The work was really done and the provider really billed for it** 5. They open `https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs`, filter to their key, and the batch is either absent or listed at `$0.00` spend 6. They check `GET https://litellm-domain/key/info` for their virtual key: `spend` is unchanged from before the batch ran 7. They wait 24 hours and repeat step 5. Still `$0.00`. Every subsequent batch they submit is also `$0.00`, indefinitely — the first un-costable batch blocks all of them 8. Their monthly budget reconciliation shows the team consumed no batch tokens at all, while the provider's own console bills them normally **After a fix: the same batches show real spend within a couple of reconciliation cycles** 1. They submit and create the batch exactly as above, receiving `200` from both calls 2. The batch is again left unpolled overnight 3. They download the results the next morning: `GET https://litellm-domain/v1/files/{output_file_id}/content` returns `200` with the real completions 4. They open `https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs`, filter to their key, and the batch is listed with a **non-zero** spend matching the tokens in the output file 5. They check `GET https://litellm-domain/key/info`: `spend` has increased by that amount 6. Batches they submit later also show real spend — an older batch that can never be priced no longer blocks the queue 7. Their monthly reconciliation matches the provider console **Authorization consequence.** Before a fix, a user whose key carries a spend cap can run batch workloads indefinitely without the cap ever being enforced, because no batch spend is ever recorded against the key: `GET https://litellm-domain/key/info` keeps reporting the pre-batch `spend`, so `max_budget` is never reached and `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/batches` keeps returning `200` past the limit. After a fix, batch spend lands against the key, so the cap applies and further batch creation is rejected once it is exhausted. ### Proof the bug occurs **Version / commit under test:** ``` image : berriai/litellm:v1.94.3 digest : sha256:b7d979bac2a9e8fbb7d55272ef5f1f4a08ab365de8f78b1800834ca718d4c941 litellm == 1.94.3 litellm-enterprise == 0.1.51 ``` **Config the proxy ran with:** ```yaml model_list: - model_name: openai-gpt-5.2 litellm_params: model: openai/gpt-5.2 api_base: os.environ/MOCK_LLM_SERVER_URL api_key: fake-key model_info: mode: batch input_cost_per_token_batches: 0.00125 output_cost_per_token_batches: 0.005 general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL proxy_batch_polling_interval: 30 litellm_settings: require_managed_files: true drop_params: true set_verbose: true ``` ``` # env DATABASE_URL=postgresql://<redacted>@db:5432/litellm PROXY_BATCH_POLLING_INTERVAL=30 MAX_OBJECTS_PER_POLL_CYCLE=2 # small so the stall is visible in minutes, not at 1,700 rows LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=<redacted> ``` Confirmed live in the container: `MAX_OBJECTS_PER_POLL_CYCLE = 2`, `MANAGED_OBJECT_STALENESS_CUTOFF_DAYS = 7`, and `proxy_server.py:8054 - Batch cost check job scheduled successfully`. #### Step 1 — the reconciler works before anything blocks it (control) A batch submitted and polled normally is costed, and `batch_processed` flips to `true`: ``` $ ./run_batch.sh $VKEY one === [one] POST /v1/files (purpose=batch) === file id: bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTphcHBsaWNhdGlvbi9qc29ubDt1bmlmaWVkX2lkLDFh... bytes : 311 purpose: batch === [one] POST /v1/batches === batch id: bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9pZDpiNDI4Yzg2NWIxYTE4MGYyMTUwMzM1Y2FlYTZkNGVjMGYyYjRjOTQ1MzZjYTQwZGYyNzIxMTQ1N2YyNWU5Yzc4O2xsbV9iYXRjaF9pZDpiYXRjaF8yMDI2MDgxMi0wNjI1LjU5Ng status : validating === [one] GET /v1/batches/{id} until completed === poll 1: status=validating request_counts={'completed': 0, 'failed': 0, 'total': 0} poll 2: status=in_progress request_counts={'completed': 2, 'failed': 0, 'total': 2} poll 3: status=completed request_counts={'completed': 2, 'failed': 0, 'total': 2} === [one] GET /v1/files/{output_file_id}/content === {"id": "batch_req_f5f35894f1cd", "custom_id": "r1", "response": {"status_code": 200, ... "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 9, "completion_tokens": 12, "total_tokens": 21}}}, "error": null} ``` ``` $ psql -c 'SELECT substring(unified_object_id,1,28) uid, status, batch_processed FROM "LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable" WHERE file_purpose='"'"'batch'"'"' ORDER BY created_at;' uid | status | batch_processed ------------------------------+-----------+----------------- bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9p | complete | t bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9p | complete | t bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9p | completed | t $ curl -s /key/info -H "Authorization: Bearer $VKEY" spend = 0.000189 ``` #### Step 2 — defect 1: seed two ids that can never resolve a model The seeded `unified_object_id` decodes to the managed-file prefix but carries no `model_id` segment, so `get_model_id_from_unified_batch_id` returns `None`: ``` $ python -c "from litellm.proxy.openai_files_endpoints.common_utils import *; \ d=_is_base64_encoded_unified_file_id('bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtsbG1fYmF0Y2hfaWQ6YmF0Y2hfb3JwaGFuX25vX21vZGVs'); \ print('decoded :', d); print('model_id:', get_model_id_from_unified_batch_id(d))" decoded : litellm_proxy;llm_batch_id:batch_orphan_no_model model_id: None ``` This is deliberately *not* the legacy `batch_<uuid>` shape: that one fails base64 decode and exits on the config-dependent branch, which correctly keeps retrying. Backdated two days so `created_at ASC` puts them at the head, and still inside the 7-day staleness window. Both rows now fill the entire `take=2` page: ``` $ psql -c 'SELECT id, status, batch_processed, created_at FROM "LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable" WHERE file_purpose='"'"'batch'"'"' AND batch_processed=false AND status NOT IN ('"'"'failed'"'"','"'"'expired'"'"','"'"'cancelled'"'"','"'"'stale_expired'"'"') ORDER BY created_at ASC LIMIT 2;' id | status | batch_processed | created_at --------------+-----------+-----------------+------------------------- b17-orphan-1 | completed | f | 2026-08-10 06:27:37.852 b17-orphan-2 | completed | f | 2026-08-10 06:27:37.852 ``` #### Step 3 — a newer batch's spend is never recorded A batch is submitted and **never polled by the client**, so reconciliation is the only path to its spend. Watched over five poll cycles: ``` cycle 1: spend=0.000567 batch-four(status/processed)=validating/false poller-queries-total=2 skip-lines=28 cycle 2: spend=0.000567 batch-four(status/processed)=validating/false poller-queries-total=2 skip-lines=30 cycle 3: spend=0.000567 batch-four(status/processed)=validating/false poller-queries-total=2 skip-lines=34 cycle 4: spend=0.000567 batch-four(status/processed)=validating/false poller-queries-total=2 skip-lines=36 cycle 5: spend=0.000567 batch-four(status/processed)=validating/false poller-queries-total=2 skip-lines=38 ``` The row never leaves `validating/false`, key spend never moves, and `poller-queries-total` is frozen at 2 (both from before the seed) while the skip-line count climbs every cycle — the reconciler spends each cycle re-reading the same two rows and reaches nothing else. ``` # the same two ids, every cycle, forever: check_batch_cost.py:138 - Skipping job bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTtsbG1fYmF0Y2hfaWQ6YmF0Y2hfb3JwaGFuX25vX21vZGVs because it is not a valid model id ``` #### Step 4 — retiring the two rows is sufficient to unblock it Marking only the two unroutable rows processed (what a fix would do) immediately lets the reconciler reach the waiting batch, on the very next cycle: ``` $ psql -c "UPDATE \"LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable\" SET batch_processed=true WHERE id IN ('b17-orphan-1','b17-orphan-2');" UPDATE 2 cycle 1: batch-four=complete/true poller-queries-total=3 <-- 2 -> 3 ``` ``` check_batch_cost.py:566 - Querying model ID: b428c865...9c78 for cost and usage of batch ID: batch_20260812-0638.572 ``` and its spend appears, having never been recorded in the ~20 minutes it sat behind the two unroutable rows: ``` $ psql -c 'SELECT to_char("startTime",'"'"'HH24:MI:SS'"'"'), call_type, spend FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" WHERE spend>0 ORDER BY "startTime";' 06:25:34 | aretrieve_batch | 0.00018375 06:25:34 | afile_content | 5.25e-06 06:27:53 | aretrieve_batch | 0.00018375 06:27:53 | afile_content | 5.25e-06 06:32:56 | aretrieve_batch | 0.00018375 06:32:56 | afile_content | 5.25e-06 06:44:42 | aretrieve_batch | 0.1425 <-- only after the head was cleared ``` #### Step 5 — defect 2: a provider 404 is retried forever A row that routes correctly (`model_id` present and resolvable) but whose provider batch record is gone. The provider 404s: ``` $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://mock-provider/v1/batches/batch_gone_from_provider 404 ``` With that row as the sole page head, over four cycles: ``` cycle 1: 404-retry log mentions=12 row=completed/false cycle 2: 404-retry log mentions=22 row=completed/false cycle 3: 404-retry log mentions=39 row=completed/false cycle 4: 404-retry log mentions=55 row=completed/false ``` ``` openai.NotFoundError: Error code: 404 - {'detail': {'error': {'message': 'No such Batch object: batch_gone_from_provider', 'type': 'invalid_request_error', 'code': 'batch_not_found'}}} 06:59:54 - check_batch_cost.py:580 - Skipping job bGl0ZWxsbV9wcm94eTttb2RlbF9pZDpiNDI4Yzg2NWIxYTE4MGYyMTUwMzM1Y2FlYTZkNGVjMGYyYjRjOTQ1MzZjYTQwZGYyNzIxMTQ1N2YyNWU5Yzc4O2xsbV9iYXRjaF9pZDpiYXRjaF9nb25lX2Zyb21fcHJvdmlkZXI because of error querying model ID: b428c865...9c78 for cost and usage of batch ID: batch_gone_from_provider: Error code: 404 - {'detail': {'error': {'message': 'No such Batch object: batch_gone_from_provider', 'type': 'invalid_request_error', 'code': 'batch_not_found'}}} ``` The row never leaves `completed/false`. The mention count grows faster than one per cycle because the router retries the 404 within a single cycle as well. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.94.3 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: feat(auth): list and revoke lite login CLI sessions from the Admin UI
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - `lite login` credentials are invisible to admins - No way to cut off a departing user's CLI access - Waiting for expiry was the only lever How it solves it: - Every CLI login registers a revocable session record - Auth refuses a revoked session within one cache interval - New CLI Sessions page lists and revokes them ## User Flow Before: an admin who needs to cut off a contractor's CLI access has no action to take, so the credential keeps working until it expires 1. The contractor runs `lite login` against https://litellm-domain and gets a working credential 2. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with it and get a 200 with a completion 3. The admin opens https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=api-keys looking for the credential and finds nothing: the Keys page lists zero keys 4. The admin has no page anywhere in the dashboard that lists CLI logins, and no revoke action to take 5. The contractor sends the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions and still gets a 200, and will keep getting one for the rest of the 24 hour lifetime After: the admin sees the login in the dashboard and revokes it, and the contractor's next request is refused 1. The contractor runs `lite login` against https://litellm-domain and gets a working credential 2. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with it and get a 200 with a completion 3. The admin opens https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=cli-sessions and sees a row for that login showing the contractor's user id, when it was issued, when it expires, and an Active badge 4. The admin clicks Revoke on that row and confirms in the dialog; the row flips to a Revoked badge 5. The contractor sends the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions and gets a 401 reading "Authentication Error - This CLI session was revoked. Run `lite login` to start a new one." Another user with their own `lite login` credential is unaffected: only the revoked login stops working, and the contractor can no longer reach any route on the proxy with it, including the management routes their role would otherwise allow ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5518 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Both runs hit a live proxy on a real Postgres against the real Anthropic API. `lite login` was driven for real, generic OIDC pointed at a throwaway local IdP, and the browser half of the device flow was followed with curl the way a browser would. ### Before, at a4ab511d0b775315730e3a328a9c490538f2949d ``` ### 1. the credential lite login just minted works against a real provider model : claude-sonnet-5 content: lit5518 before-leg live usage : 36 tokens ### 2. an admin looks for an operator surface listing CLI sessions GET /cli/session/list -> http=404 {"detail":"Not Found"} ### 3. the session is not on the Keys page either virtual keys on the proxy : 0 any of them a CLI session : False ### 4. nothing server side records the session, so nothing can be revoked rows in LiteLLM_CLISessionTable: 0 ### 5. the only lever is expiry: the credential still works POST /v1/chat/completions -> http=200 ``` ### After, at 6dd0fa5146 (captured at d8a4cad1e5, whose proxy code this commit only rebases) ``` ### 1. the credential lite login just minted works against a real provider model : claude-sonnet-5 content: lit5518 after-leg live usage : 36 tokens ### 2. the session is now visible to an operator { "sessions": [ { "session_id": "12aebc0f018f192c5225dee036a5e8b730ca21e5d3b0d359ea80df0a1a5ce362", "user_id": "lit5518-user", "team_id": null, "created_at": "2026-08-13T23:42:29.788000Z", "expires_at": "2026-08-14T23:42:29.787000Z", "revoked_at": null, "revoked_by": null } ], "total_count": 1 } ### 3. revoke it (this is the request the dashboard Revoke button sends) a probe runs every 200ms against the same auth path while the revoke lands probes before the revoke, all 200 : 12 last 200 seen : -0.16s relative to the revoke first 401 seen : +0.10s relative to the revoke probes after the first 401 that were 200 again: 0 ### 4. the same credential is now refused, with the reason POST /v1/chat/completions -> http=401 type : auth_error message: Authentication Error - This CLI session was revoked. Run `lite login` to start a new one. ``` ### Orderings and principals checked on the same live proxy ``` ### a session revoked BEFORE it was ever used revoke -> http=200 first ever request -> http=401 message: Authentication Error - This CLI session was revoked. Run `lite login` to start a new one. ### a third login is unaffected: revocation is per session, not a blanket block third session -> http=200 content: lit5518 third session live ### role gating, through the real route layer rather than the handler alone GET /cli/session/list as proxy_admin_viewer -> http=200 POST .../revoke as proxy_admin_viewer -> http=403 POST .../revoke as a named proxy_admin -> http=200, revoked_by "lit5518-user" ``` ### UI The dashboard half is a new CLI Sessions entry in the AI Gateway section of the left nav, admin only, at `?page=cli-sessions`. Chrome automation was unavailable on the capture box, so the still needs a hand: run the proxy, run `npm run dev` in `ui/litellm-dashboard`, open the CLI Sessions page after a `lite login`, and the row with its Revoke button is the shot. ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats (if any) - Sessions minted before this change keep working until expiry - Revocation is per session; there is no revoke-all-for-user yet - Convergence on other replicas is bounded by `DEFAULT_IN_MEMORY_TTL` - Expired session rows are hidden from the list but never pruned ## Review notes Both Greptile findings were real and both were taken. The first, that a valid CLI credential could fail whenever its revocation cache missed during a Prisma outage, was the sharper one: this credential previously authenticated with no database read at all on the admin path, so a lookup that raises is a new failure mode. The lookup now routes any failure through `PrismaDBExceptionHandler.handle_db_exception`, which is the proxy's existing seam for exactly this decision, so an operator who set `allow_requests_on_db_unavailable` keeps serving CLI sessions during an outage and one who did not gets the same failure every other DB-backed auth read already gives, rather than a private policy invented here. The second, that the page offered a Revoke control to roles the backend refuses, took two passes and the review was right to reject the first one. `effectiveSessionRole` normalizes `proxy_admin_viewer` to `Admin` so read parity works, which means a role-only check cannot tell a revoker from a reader; the gate now also requires `!isViewOnly`, the signal the rest of the dashboard already uses for exactly this. The page, the list query and the nav entry separately moved off `all_admin_roles`, which carries org admin, whom the proxy refuses on tenant-wide reads. Two findings were not taken. The docs one asks for the revocation guidance to move to litellm-docs; the sentence I changed is a pre-existing in-repo claim that this PR makes false, quoted verbatim in the ticket as evidence, so correcting it in place is the smaller and more honest change and relocating the surrounding product docs is its own piece of work. The unbounded-registry one is real but not a new exposure: a row is only written by a completed SSO login, the same act that already mints a credential, and rows are bounded by that same authenticated flow. A retention sweep for expired sessions is worth doing and is listed as a caveat rather than smuggled into this PR. The revocation lookup is cached in the shared auth `DualCache` rather than read per request, so a CLI session costs one indexed read per cache interval per replica instead of one per request. The pod that serves the revoke publishes the revoked state into that cache directly, which is why the capture shows the first 401 arriving 0.15s after the revoke rather than at the TTL boundary; a replica that did not serve the revoke picks it up from Redis once its own entry lapses, which is the `DEFAULT_IN_MEMORY_TTL` bound quoted above. There is no second cache to invalidate: a CLI credential never enters the key cache, because the only write-back on that path fires after a database load and a self-contained blob never gets one. Registration is deliberately fail-closed and revocation deliberately fail-open on a missing row. A login that cannot be recorded is never handed to the CLI, since it could never be revoked; a session with no row at all predates this change and keeps authenticating until it expires, so upgrading does not sign every CLI user out. ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR
