signal.title: [Bug] Databricks provider sends internal `thinking_blocks` field instead of the documented `reasoning` content block, breaking multi-turn extended thinking
signal.text: **LiteLLM version:** v1.96.0 **Provider:** `databricks` (Azure Databricks Foundation Model API) **Models:** `system.ai.claude-opus-5`, `system.ai.claude-sonnet-5` ## What happens Multi-turn conversations with extended thinking fail as soon as an assistant message containing thinking content is replayed as history: ``` litellm.BadRequestError: DatabricksException - {"error_code":"BAD_REQUEST", "message":"{\"message\":\"messages.98.thinking_blocks: Extra inputs are not permitted\"}"} ``` The first turn always succeeds. The failing index tracks conversation length — it is whichever message is the first assistant turn carrying thinking content. ## Cause `litellm/llms/databricks/chat/transformation.py` (~line 499) extracts reasoning content from Databricks responses into LiteLLM's internal `thinking_blocks` representation. There is no corresponding conversion on the **request** path, so on the next turn `thinking_blocks` is emitted as a message-level field. Databricks validates strictly and rejects unknown message fields. ## This is not a Databricks limitation Databricks accepts reasoning content on input. I verified the wire format empirically by capturing a real reasoning block from `system.ai.claude-opus-5` and replaying it in each candidate shape. Only one is accepted: | Assistant content block shape | Result | | --- | --- | | `{"type": "thinking", "thinking": ..., "signature": ...}` (Anthropic native) | rejected, `Failed to parse ContentItem` | | `{"type": "reasoning", "content": [{"type": "reasoning_text", ...}], "encrypted_content": ...}` | rejected, `Expecting one non-null Summary` | | `{"type": "reasoning", "summary": [{"type": "summary_text", "text": ..., "signature": ...}]}` | **accepted** | | message-level `thinking_blocks` (current behaviour) | rejected, `Extra inputs are not permitted` | So the target format is a `reasoning` content block carrying a `summary` array: ```json { "type": "reasoning", "summary": [ { "type": "summary_text", "text": "...", "signature": "<opaque provider signature>" } ] } ``` Note that Databricks' published docs for multi-turn reasoning describe `content` / `reasoning_text` with `encrypted_content`, which the endpoint actively rejects. The shape asserted by the existing test in `tests/test_litellm/llms/databricks/chat/test_databricks_chat_transformation.py` is the correct one, and matches what the provider's own response parsing already produces The `signature` must be replayed unmodified. Dropping it loses the reasoning chain even when the request is accepted ## Expected behaviour On the request path, the Databricks provider should convert LiteLLM `thinking_blocks` into the documented `reasoning` content block, mapping the Anthropic thinking `signature` to `encrypted_content` so reasoning continuity is preserved. Note that **merely stripping `thinking_blocks` is only a partial fix**: it clears the 400 but discards the reasoning chain, which is the behaviour Databricks explicitly describes as "the model can't reason over its earlier thinking." ## Control The Anthropic provider round-trips thinking correctly in the same LiteLLM version, with the same client and the same conversation — only the `databricks` provider fails. So the round trip is clearly within LiteLLM's remit. ## Related prior issues - **#15758** — same error. Closed by the reporter within a day, attributing it to Databricks (*"this is a Databricks issue and cannot be fixed with code"*). Per the documentation above, that attribution is incorrect and the bug is still present. - **#9790** — feature request for exactly this, went stale and was auto-closed. The reporter there used `summary` / `summary_text`, which is not the documented schema either, so that failure was also a format mismatch rather than a missing feature. ## Reproduction 1. Configure a `databricks` deployment for `system.ai.claude-opus-5`. 2. Send a request with extended thinking enabled. 3. Append the assistant response, including reasoning content, to the message list. 4. Send a second request with that history → 400 as above. ## Environment note Requests reach the endpoint via `/ai-gateway/mlflow/v1/chat/completions`. Separately observed on the same models: `temperature`, `top_p`, and `top_k` are rejected with 400 by both `claude-opus-5` and `claude-sonnet-5` (Databricks documents this for Sonnet 5 only). Not related to this bug, but relevant to anyone configuring these deployments — `drop_params` handles it.

signal.title: perf(vertex): use list buffer for accumulated JSON streaming shards
signal.text: ## Relevant issues Fixes #31861 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes lint/format for the changed lines and unit tests pass locally - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem ## Type 🚄 Infrastructure (performance) ## What / Why `ModelResponseIterator.handle_accumulated_json_chunk` (Vertex/Gemini streaming) accumulated partial JSON with `self.accumulated_json += message` on every SSE shard. Because `self` also holds a reference to that string, CPython **cannot** take the in-place concatenation fast path and must copy the entire prior buffer on every shard — making buffer *assembly* **O(n²)** in total payload size. For a multi-MB Gemini tool-call response split across thousands of ~2 KB shards, this copies gigabytes before the single `json.loads`, showing up as elevated asyncio event-loop latency proportional to payload size. (This is the buffer-assembly companion to the `json.loads`-frequency fix in #31297 / #26181, which addressed the parse side of the same function.) ## The fix Store shards in a `list[str]` (`accumulated_json_chunks`) and `"".join()` **once** when the completeness heuristic passes — O(n) total instead of O(n²). - The tail check (only attempt `json.loads` once a shard closes a JSON value) now inspects the **last shard**, which is O(1), instead of `rstrip()`-ing the whole joined buffer on every fragment. - The end-of-stream **flush** (`chunk == ""`) always attempts a parse, so a complete buffer is never dropped even if the final shard were whitespace-only (correctness safeguard). - A backward-compatible `accumulated_json` **str property** (getter joins, setter replaces) preserves the previous read/write interface for any caller/subclass referencing it directly — including the existing truthiness checks in `__next__`/`__anext__`. ## Test Added a `TestAccumulatedJsonBuffer` class in the existing Vertex/Gemini test file (mocked, no API calls): - `test_sharded_json_accumulates_and_parses` — a JSON object split across 23 shards parses on the final shard and resets the buffer - `test_incomplete_buffer_returns_none_without_reset` — fragments that don't close a value keep accumulating - `test_flush_parses_buffer_with_trailing_whitespace_shard` — the flush safeguard recovers a complete buffer even when the last shard is whitespace-only - `test_accumulated_json_property_backward_compat` — the `str` property still reads/writes the list buffer ```bash uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/llms/vertex_ai/gemini/test_vertex_and_google_ai_studio_gemini.py -q # 137 passed (127 pre-existing + 4 new + 6 in the streaming tool-call file) ``` ## Proof of Fix Microbenchmark driving `handle_accumulated_json_chunk` with 4000 shards of 2 KB each (the issue's reproducer scenario), measuring buffer assembly: ``` BEFORE (str += per shard): ~596 ms AFTER (list buffer): ~4 ms ``` ~130–200x faster buffer assembly, and it no longer holds the GIL/event loop proportional to payload size. Correctness is covered by the 137 passing unit tests above (the sharded-parse test asserts the exact same parsed output as before).

signal.title: [Bug]: SSO and JWT email matching can take over an existing proxy admin
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate ### What happened? When an SSO or JWT subject does not match an existing `user_id` or `sso_user_id`, LiteLLM falls back to a case-insensitive email lookup. A matching row is returned even if it already has a different `sso_user_id`, and LiteLLM schedules an update that overwrites that id with the new subject The SSO path then inherits the matched row's stored role when the identity provider did not supply a LiteLLM role. The JWT path checks the matched row's role directly. A different identity-provider subject that can present an existing privileged email can therefore inherit `PROXY_ADMIN` and durably rebind the victim's `sso_user_id` There is no shared requirement that the email claim is verified, no refusal when the row already has a different SSO subject, and no protection for administrative roles Expected behavior is that email linking is allowed only for a verified email on an explicitly unlinked or invited row. A row already bound to another subject, especially a proxy admin, must not be silently rebound ### User Flow Before a fix: a second identity-provider subject can become an existing proxy admin by presenting the same email 1. An administrator already has a LiteLLM dashboard account bound to SSO subject `admin-subject` 2. A different trusted identity-provider subject authenticates at `GET https://litellm-domain/sso/callback` with the administrator's email in its claims 3. LiteLLM misses by the new subject, finds the administrator row by email, and overwrites its `sso_user_id` 4. The new subject is redirected into `https://litellm-domain/ui/` with the stored `proxy_admin` role 5. The new subject can call `POST https://litellm-domain/key/generate` and other administrator routes 6. The original administrator can be locked out because their row is now bound to the different subject 7. The attacker can access other users' keys and management data that their original identity should never reach After a fix: a subject mismatch cannot silently link to a privileged or already-bound row 1. The same administrator account remains bound to `admin-subject` 2. The different identity-provider subject authenticates with the same email claim 3. LiteLLM detects that the row is already bound to another subject, or that the email is not verified 4. `GET https://litellm-domain/sso/callback` returns a 403 or creates a separate non-admin user according to policy 5. The new subject cannot call `POST https://litellm-domain/key/generate` 6. The original administrator remains able to sign in with `admin-subject` 7. The second subject cannot read or modify any other user's management objects ### Proof the bug occurs Config / setup: ```yaml general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL ``` Enable Generic OIDC, SAML, or JWT auth. Existing database row: ```json { "user_id": "admin-user", "user_email": "admin@example.test", "sso_user_id": "admin-subject", "user_role": "proxy_admin" } ``` Version / commit: ```text v1.98.0, commit 46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff ``` Current shared fuzzy-link code: ```python if response is None and user_email is not None: response = await user_table.find_first( where={"user_email": {"equals": user_email, "mode": "insensitive"}}, include={"organization_memberships": True}, ) if response is not None and sso_user_id is not None: asyncio.create_task( user_table.update( where={"user_id": response.user_id}, data={"sso_user_id": sso_user_id}, ) ) ``` The repository's existing test encodes the unsafe rebinding contract. It starts with a row whose SSO id is `sso_123`, looks it up by email for `new_sso_456`, and expects the update to the new id Audit command and output: ```shell $ uv run --no-sync python -m pytest tests/proxy_unit_tests/test_auth_checks.py::test_get_fuzzy_user_object ============================== 1 passed ============================== ``` The current SSO role resolution uses the database role when the SSO response does not supply a LiteLLM role. The JWT auth builder also calls `get_user_object` with the presented subject and email, then treats a returned `PROXY_ADMIN` row as admin A live third-party identity provider was not used because reproducing against a real account would modify authentication state. The test and source path confirm the email match, subject overwrite, and role inheritance without external side effects ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.98.0, commit 46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: [Bug]: budget_limits reset clears Redis before reset_at commits
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate ### What happened? The multi-window budget reset path clears each Redis enforcement counter before it persists the window's new `reset_at` in PostgreSQL `_reset_expired_window` sets the in-memory and Redis counter to `0.0`, mutates the local JSON, and returns. `reset_budget_windows` performs the database update afterwards. If that update fails, the database still says the old window is due while Redis authoritatively reports zero spend The reservation path treats a Redis zero as a warm cache hit, so it does not reconstruct the old window's spend from logs. A fully spent window can receive another full budget. A later reset tick can clear the replacement spend again Expected behavior is commit first, then clear or delete the enforcement counter only for a window whose `reset_at` advance succeeded ### User Flow Before a fix: a key receives a second full budget when the reset database update fails 1. The user has a key with a `budget_limits` window of `$10/day`, has spent `$10`, and its `reset_at` is due 2. The reset job sets `spend:key:<token>:window:1d` to zero 3. The PostgreSQL update of `budget_limits.reset_at` times out, so the stored window is still due 4. The user sends `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions` for a request costing `$1` 5. The proxy reads the warm zero counter, increments it to one, and returns 200 6. The user can spend another `$9` in the same still-due window, exceeding the original limit 7. Another caller using the same key shares that unintended headroom After a fix: a failed reset write leaves the old enforcement counter intact 1. The user has the same fully spent `$10/day` window and due `reset_at` 2. The reset job computes the future `reset_at` but the PostgreSQL update times out 3. Redis remains at `10`, or the missing counter is reconstructed from spend logs for the old window 4. The user sends the same `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions` 5. The proxy rejects the request because the old window is still exhausted 6. After a later successful database update, Redis is cleared for the new window 7. The user can spend up to `$10` in that new window and no more ### Proof the bug occurs Config / setup: ```yaml general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL ``` Create a key or team whose `budget_limits` JSON contains a due window and whose corresponding Redis counter is already at its maximum Version / commit: ```text v1.98.0, commit 46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff ``` Current order in `_reset_expired_window`: ```python spend_counter_cache.in_memory_cache.set_cache(key=counter_key, value=0.0) if spend_counter_cache.redis_cache is not None: await spend_counter_cache.redis_cache.async_set_cache( key=counter_key, value=0.0, ) window["reset_at"] = compute_budget_reset_at(...).isoformat() return True ``` Only after that helper returns does `reset_budget_windows` call: ```python await VerificationTokenRepository(self.prisma_client).table.update( where={"token": row["token"]}, data={"budget_limits": windows}, ) ``` The same class documents the required opposite order for ordinary key, user, and team spend counters: clear Redis only after the database write commits The audit confirmed Redis is set before the database update and that a value of `0.0` is considered a warm cache hit. A live failure injection against PostgreSQL was not run, but raising from the later update leaves the already-written Redis zero with no compensating action ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.98.0, commit 46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: [Bug]: Concurrent budget reset jobs erase spend from the new window
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate ### What happened? Every proxy replica schedules `ResetBudgetJob.reset_budget`. The job reads due keys, users, and teams and later performs unconditional updates that set `spend=0` and advance `budget_reset_at` There is no `PodLockManager` lock around the reset tick and no compare-and-swap condition on the old `budget_reset_at`. Two replicas can read the same due row. If replica A resets it, new-window traffic increments spend, and replica B then applies its stale reset, replica B erases the new-window spend from PostgreSQL and zeros the Redis counter Both reset jobs report success. The affected key, user, or team appears to have a full budget even though it has already spent in the new window Expected behavior is that one reset wins per entity and a stale second writer cannot erase spend recorded after that reset ### User Flow Before a fix: a virtual-key user can spend past the new-window budget after two replicas reset the same key 1. The user has a virtual key with a `$10` daily budget and the previous window is due for reset 2. Two proxy replicas start their reset jobs and both read the key as due 3. Replica A commits the reset 4. The user sends `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions` and receives 200 for a request costing `$2` 5. Replica B commits its stale `spend=0` update and clears the Redis counter 6. `GET https://litellm-domain/key/info` reports `spend: 0` for the new window 7. The user can send another `$10` of requests before receiving a budget rejection, exceeding the intended window by the erased amount After a fix: only one reset can advance the due row and post-reset spend remains visible 1. The user has the same virtual key and due daily budget 2. Two proxy replicas start their reset jobs 3. One replica atomically advances the due row and the second updates zero rows 4. The user sends the same `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions` and receives 200 for a `$2` request 5. `GET https://litellm-domain/key/info` reports `spend: 2` 6. A further `$8` reaches the budget, and a request that would exceed `$10` is rejected 7. Another user cannot consume budget headroom created by a stale reset ### Proof the bug occurs Config / setup: ```yaml general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL ``` Run at least two proxy replicas with `disable_reset_budget` unset. Give a key, user, or team a `budget_duration` and a due `budget_reset_at` Version / commit: ```text v1.98.0, commit 46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff ``` Current reset tick: ```python await self.reset_budget_for_litellm_keys() await self.reset_budget_for_litellm_users() await self.reset_budget_for_litellm_teams() await self.reset_budget_for_litellm_budget_table() await self.reset_budget_windows() ``` Current queued writes in `litellm/repositories/unit_of_work.py`: ```python self.table.update( where={"token": token}, data={"spend": 0, "budget_reset_at": budget_reset_at}, ) ``` The user and team writes have the same unconditional shape. There is no lock acquisition in `reset_budget_job.py`, and the write does not require the row to remain due The deterministic database ordering is: ```text A: UPDATE spend=0, budget_reset_at=future request: UPDATE spend = spend + 2 B: UPDATE spend=0, budget_reset_at=future final spend: 0 ``` A live two-pod proxy was not started during this audit. The lost update is the direct result of two unconditional successful writes around an increment ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.98.0, commit 46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: [Bug]: CheckBatchCost can apply completed batch spend more than once
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate ### What happened? The enterprise `CheckBatchCost` poller applies the full cost of a completed managed batch before it writes `batch_processed=true`. The spend side effect and the processed flag are not atomic, the flag update is not compare-and-swap, and the poller has no cross-pod lock If the final managed-object update fails, the next poll selects the same `batch_processed=false` row and bills it again. If two proxy replicas select the row concurrently, both can emit spend before either writes the flag The emitted success callback increments live Redis budget counters and queues SQL increments for key, user, team, organization, end-user, and daily spend. A duplicate spend-log request id does not roll those other increments back Expected behavior is exactly-once accounting for each managed batch, including concurrent pollers and retry after a database timeout ### User Flow Before a fix: a batch user is charged twice when two pollers reconcile the same completed batch 1. The user uploads JSONL with `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/files` and receives a managed file id 2. The user creates a batch with `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/batches` and receives a managed batch id 3. The provider completes the batch once 4. Two proxy replicas poll the still-unprocessed managed row and each records the full batch cost 5. The user opens `https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs` and sees duplicated or inconsistent batch accounting 6. `GET https://litellm-domain/key/info` reports spend increased by up to twice the provider cost 7. A later `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/batches` can be rejected because the duplicated increment exhausted the user's budget After a fix: only one poller can claim and account for the completed batch 1. The user uploads the same JSONL and creates the same batch 2. The provider completes the batch once 3. Two proxy replicas attempt reconciliation 4. One replica atomically claims the managed row and the other observes that it is already claimed 5. `https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs` shows one billed batch 6. `GET https://litellm-domain/key/info` increases by exactly the provider cost 7. Later batch creation is blocked only when real spend reaches the configured budget ### Proof the bug occurs Config / setup: ```yaml general_settings: proxy_batch_polling_interval: 3600 litellm_settings: require_managed_files: true ``` Two or more proxy replicas share the same `DATABASE_URL`. `PROXY_BATCH_POLLING_ENABLED` is left at its default enabled value Version / commit: ```text v1.98.0, commit 46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff ``` Current control-flow order in `enterprise/litellm_enterprise/proxy/common_utils/check_batch_cost.py`: ```python tracked = await self._track_completed_batch_cost(...) processed_models.append(tracked) update_data = { "status": "complete", "file_object": response.model_dump_json(), } update_data["batch_processed"] = True await self.prisma_client.db.litellm_managedobjecttable.update( where={"id": job.id}, data=update_data, ) ``` The update failure is logged and swallowed after the spend callback has run: ```python except Exception as db_err: verbose_proxy_logger.error( f"CheckBatchCost: failed to mark job {job.id} complete in DB: {db_err}" ) ``` The initial read is a normal `find_many` with `batch_processed=False`. There is no `PodLockManager`, processing lease, or conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE batch_processed=false` in this file The audit confirmed the emit line precedes the mark line and that each tracking call creates a new callback context. A live provider batch was not submitted during this audit because that would incur external cost. The race and retry are deterministic from the persisted ordering above ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.98.0, commit 46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: [Bug]: Helm upgrade rolls new proxy pods before the migration Job completes
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate ### What happened? The published `helm/litellm-helm` chart defaults `migrationJob.enabled=true` and `migrationJob.hooks.helm.enabled=false`. The Deployment also forces `DISABLE_SCHEMA_UPDATE=true`, so application pods cannot migrate the database themselves On `helm upgrade`, the migration Job is therefore an ordinary resource rather than a pre-upgrade hook. Helm can update the Deployment and start the new image before the Job has completed. The new Prisma client then queries columns introduced by that image while the database still has the previous release's schema The default replica count is one. A normal schema-bearing upgrade can replace the only serving pod with an N+1 binary against an N schema. Readiness can still pass because it does not verify every ORM model column Expected behavior is that schema expansion completes before any N+1 proxy replica starts serving. The componentized `helm/litellm` chart already uses a `pre-install,pre-upgrade` migration hook This is not a duplicate of #7536, which reports an existing non-hook Job not being recreated, or #16190, which reports the migration Job starting before a newly deployed database is reachable ### User Flow Before a fix: a Helm operator gets a Ready N+1 pod while the database still has the N schema 1. The operator runs `helm upgrade litellm oci://ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-helm --set image.tag=<N+1>` with the chart defaults 2. Kubernetes starts the N+1 Deployment pod with `DISABLE_SCHEMA_UPDATE=true` 3. The migration Job has not completed yet, but `GET https://litellm-domain/health/readiness` returns 200 4. The operator sends `GET https://litellm-domain/model/info` or `GET https://litellm-domain/key/list` 5. The request returns a database error for an N+1 column that does not exist yet 6. The same route starts working only after the migration Job finishes, or remains broken if that Job fails After a fix: Helm completes the schema expansion before creating any N+1 proxy pod 1. The operator runs the same `helm upgrade` command with the same image and values 2. Helm runs the migration Job as a blocking pre-upgrade hook 3. The Job applies the N+1 migration and exits successfully 4. Kubernetes then starts the N+1 Deployment pod 5. `GET https://litellm-domain/health/readiness` returns 200 only after the compatible pod is running 6. `GET https://litellm-domain/model/info` and `GET https://litellm-domain/key/list` return 200 throughout the serving transition ### Proof the bug occurs Config / setup: ```yaml replicaCount: 1 migrationJob: enabled: true hooks: argocd: enabled: true helm: enabled: false ``` Version / commit: ```text v1.98.0, commit 46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff ``` Current template evidence: ```yaml {{- if .Values.migrationJob.hooks.helm.enabled }} helm.sh/hook: "pre-install,pre-upgrade" helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: "before-hook-creation" {{- end }} ``` The Deployment separately emits: ```yaml {{- if .Values.migrationJob.enabled }} - name: DISABLE_SCHEMA_UPDATE value: "true" {{- end }} ``` With the default values, the Job has no Helm hook annotation and the proxy cannot close the schema gap. The generated Prisma models include additive fields such as `LiteLLM_Config.last_run_at` and `reload_revision`. Querying those fields against the previous schema produces PostgreSQL's `column does not exist` error The audit reproduced the database half of the transition by removing those additive columns from a migrated disposable PostgreSQL database and issuing the N+1 SELECT list: ```sql SELECT "param_name", "param_value", "last_run_at", "reload_revision" FROM "LiteLLM_Config" WHERE "param_name" = 'general_settings'; ``` ```text ERROR: column "last_run_at" does not exist ``` A Kubernetes cluster was not available in this audit, so the Helm ordering itself was confirmed from rendered-resource conditions and Helm's ordinary-resource lifecycle rather than a live `helm upgrade` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.98.0, commit 46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: [Bug]: Required PR checks can pass when schema.prisma has no matching migration
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate ### What happened? A pull request can change `schema.prisma` without adding equivalent SQL under `litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations`, and the required GitHub Actions path can still pass The only test that asks Prisma whether the committed migration history produces the current datamodel is `tests/proxy_migration_tests/test_db_schema_migration.py`. It skips without `DATABASE_URL`, and no GitHub Actions unit job starts Postgres for it The GitHub Actions substitute, `test_aaaaaschema_compatibility`, runs `git show main:schema.prisma` but does not check the command's exit status. The reusable unit workflow uses the default depth-1 checkout, so `main` is normally absent. The missing schema becomes an empty string, the old-model map becomes empty, and the test reports no breaking changes Even with a full `main` ref, the test treats a newly added required field as informational. That is the common failure mode where the generated client expects a column that no migration creates Expected behavior is a required pull-request check that applies all committed migrations to an empty PostgreSQL database and fails when `prisma migrate diff --from-url ... --to-schema-datamodel schema.prisma --exit-code` detects drift ### User Flow Before a fix: a proxy operator upgrades to a release whose generated client expects a column that the shipped migrations never created 1. A maintainer merges a pull request after every required GitHub Actions check passes 2. The operator deploys that release and its migration Job completes because there is no new SQL migration to apply 3. The operator sends `GET https://litellm-domain/key/list` with an admin key 4. The proxy queries through the new generated client and returns a 500 database error because the expected column is missing 5. Requests that touch the affected model continue failing until the operator authors and applies corrective SQL After a fix: the same incomplete schema pull request is blocked before an operator can deploy it 1. A maintainer opens the same pull request with a `schema.prisma` field and no matching SQL migration 2. The required migration-diff job creates an empty PostgreSQL database and applies every committed migration 3. Prisma reports datamodel drift and the pull request check fails 4. The maintainer adds the missing migration and the check passes 5. The operator upgrades and `GET https://litellm-domain/key/list` returns 200 against the migrated schema ### Proof the bug occurs Config / setup: ```text GitHub Actions reusable unit workflow: .github/workflows/_test-unit-base.yml Checkout: actions/checkout with no fetch-depth override Migration oracle: tests/proxy_migration_tests/test_db_schema_migration.py ``` Version / commit: ```text v1.98.0, commit 46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff ``` Deterministic evidence from the current tree: ```python def get_schema_from_branch(branch: str = "main") -> str: result = subprocess.run( ["git", "show", f"{branch}:schema.prisma"], capture_output=True, text=True, ) return result.stdout ``` The caller parses that returned string without checking `result.returncode`. On the depth-1 checkout shape used by the workflow, the audit reproduced: ```shell $ git show main:schema.prisma fatal: invalid object name 'main' $ python -c 'from tests.proxy_unit_tests.test_db_schema_changes import get_schema_from_branch, parse_model_fields; print(repr(get_schema_from_branch("main"))); print(parse_model_fields(get_schema_from_branch("main")))' '' {} ``` The actual migration oracle is explicitly disabled without a database: ```python @pytest.mark.skipif( "DATABASE_URL" not in os.environ, reason="requires a postgres database (DATABASE_URL)", ) ``` The current GitHub Actions workflows do not set `DATABASE_URL` for that test. CircleCI has a PostgreSQL-backed `schema_migration_check`, but it is not the required GitHub Actions pull-request gate This validation did not deploy a live proxy because the defect is in pull-request assurance. The production consequence follows when an incomplete schema change is merged and deployed ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Other ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.98.0, commit 46ffc2ab7d4b29889b54f9ccefd78f995a0e53ff ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: Fix/notfound error retries
signal.text: Fixes #36896 ## What this does `RetryPolicy` had a retry count field for every exception type except `NotFoundError` (404s). Because of that gap, 404s always fall back to `num_retries`, so the router retries them — and since 404 also triggers an immediate cooldown per deployment, each retry cools down another deployment. After enough retries the whole pool gets cooled and the router raises `RouterRateLimitError("No deployments available")`, which surfaces to the client as a 500. This adds a `NotFoundErrorRetries` field so operators can set it to `0` and have 404s returned to the client immediately instead of being retried across the whole deployment pool. ## Changes - `litellm/types/router.py`: added `NotFoundErrorRetries: int | None = None` to `RetryPolicy`. - `litellm/router_utils/get_retry_from_policy.py`: imported `NotFoundError` and added a check in `get_num_retries_from_retry_policy()` so `NotFoundErrorRetries` is respected. - `tests/router_unit_tests/test_router_helper_utils.py`: added a `NotFoundError` case to the existing `test_get_num_retries_from_retry_policy` parametrized test, using `0` retries to match the motivating case from the issue. ## Testing Ran the existing parametrized test locally — all cases pass including the new `NotFoundError` one. Note: this PR only addresses the missing retry field (the primary fix requested in the issue). The secondary "paradox" behavior mentioned in the issue (an exception that triggers cooldown also being retried by default) is a broader behavioral change and is left out of scope here.

signal.title: LiteLLM Stability Sprint Roadmap
signal.text: Hi all, we are treating stability as a first class citizen. Sharing our roadmap for bug fixes and stability improvements planned over this week. Please comment what bugs you'd like to see fixed over this sprint ## AI Engineering - LLM Translation - [x] `/v1/model/info` returns inconsistent responses for team-based models, so team-scoped model metadata needs to be reconciled. - [ ] Container/code-interpreter file retrieval on Azure fails for service-account virtual keys (403 / "no persisted bytes available"), so file content fetches need to work end-to-end under scoped non-admin keys. (LIT-3769) - [ ] Streaming file uploads fail with agents SDK in v1.88.0 on /v1/responses API (LIT-3737) - [x] Bedrock Mantle not working for OpenAI (Urgent Bug/Blocker) ## Spend Tracking and Budgets - [ ] P0: Virtual key spend limits are not being enforced (LIT-3772) - [x] P0: Anthropic cost tracking is inaccurate for cached and tiered usage (LIT-3771) ## UI + Auth - [ ] Budget reset timing isn't recalculated correctly when the duration changes. (LIT-3362) - [x] Add verification_uri_complete to CLI SSO device flow (LIT-3693) (Urgent Blocking Bug/Regression) ## Performance - [x] Guardrails continuously reinitialize, causing runner leaks, latency spikes, and OOMs that need to be eliminated. - [x] Rate limiting under Custom Auth isn't enforcing model-level limits correctly and needs to apply per-model caps reliably. ## Logging & Guardrails - [x] `async_pre_call_hook` fires twice per request on CustomGuardrail, so the duplicate invocation needs to be collapsed to a single call. - [x] AIM for Guardrails corrupts Google ADK session state, so guardrail processing must stop mutating or clobbering session data. (LIT-3751) - [x] OpenTelemetry metrics high-cardinality attributes trigger Splunk throttling. (LIT-3600) ## Larger Stability Bets Beyond the week's fixes, we're making two structural bets to drive down whole classes of bugs. ### Auth & Identity Resolution DRI: @yassin-berriai **Problem:** Identity resolution and authorization are flaky. Resolving caller identity currently takes 5+ DB calls, and bugs here show up as missing team IDs in traces or spend not being attributed to a team. **Root cause:** Caller identity is resolved piecemeal across separate code paths that each independently fetch key, team, user, org, end-user, and project objects instead of resolving identity once into a single typed object. Because those fetches are error-isolated, a partial lookup degrades silently rather than failing loud, so team_id quietly drops out and the request still proceeds. There is no single source of truth for "who is this caller" that both authorization and logging consume. **The bet:** If we resolve caller identity exactly once into a single typed object that every downstream check and logger consumes, we cut identity-resolution DB calls roughly in half and get fewer than 1 identity-attribution bug per release. ### MCP Gateway Credentials & OAuth DRI: @tin-berri **Problem:** Users report being unable to view tools or authenticate for MCP servers across different server configurations on the Gateway and Claude Code. **Root cause:** There are five parallel credential paths plus an override cascade with no single resolver, and `list` and `call` signatures that don't match, so the credential a user gets depends on the entry point. A stripped header can silently downgrade auth, leaving the server configuration or user credentials unregistered and returning no tools. Tokens are also cached as effectively non-expiring and never refreshed, on top of a hand-rolled OAuth surface (fake DCR, no state TTL/nonce). **The bet:** If we replace the cascade with one fail-closed `resolve((subject, server))` per declared mode and one normalized token store with proactive and reactive refresh, the OAuth/credential bug class drops to near zero.

signal.title: [Bug] Databricks provider drops Anthropic prompt-cache token counts when streaming
signal.text: **LiteLLM version:** v1.96.0 (also reproduced on v1.90.2) **Provider:** `databricks` (Azure Databricks Foundation Model API, Claude models) **Model:** `system.ai.claude-opus-5` ## What happens With `stream: false`, prompt-cache token counts are returned correctly. With `stream: true`, `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` are absent from the usage object entirely — not zero, absent. Because spend is computed from the usage object, every streamed Databricks request is costed at the full input rate even when it was served from cache. For an Anthropic-format agent client that always streams and relies on prompt caching, this makes reported spend diverge sharply from actual provider cost. Importantly, **caching itself works** — only the accounting is broken. See "Caching is actually working" below. ## Reproduction Identical payload, only `stream` differs. Fallbacks and retries disabled. ```python body = { "model": "claude-opus", # -> databricks/system.ai.claude-opus-5 "max_tokens": 8, "system": [{"type": "text", "text": CORPUS, # ~9.6k tokens "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}], "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with OK."}], "disable_fallbacks": True, "num_retries": 0, } ``` **Non-streaming — correct:** ``` 1st (cold) input_tokens=11 cache_creation_input_tokens=9603 cache_read_input_tokens=None 2nd (warm) input_tokens=11 cache_creation_input_tokens=None cache_read_input_tokens=9603 ``` **Streaming — cache fields missing from every event:** ``` message_start usage: {"input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": ...} message_delta usage: {"input_tokens": 11, "output_tokens": 1} ``` ### Same-endpoint control, with `stream_options` To rule out `stream_options` as the cause, the following ran against `/v1/chat/completions` with `"stream_options": {"include_usage": true}` on both providers — identical payload, identical proxy, only the provider differs: ``` anthropic cold prompt_tokens_details: {"cached_tokens": 0, "text_tokens": 10, "cache_write_tokens": ...} anthropic warm prompt_tokens_details: {"cached_tokens": 13304, "text_tokens": 10, "cache_write_tokens": ...} databricks cold (no prompt_tokens_details) prompt_tokens: 7015 databricks warm (no prompt_tokens_details) prompt_tokens: 7015 ``` The Anthropic provider is correct in both streaming and non-streaming modes. Note also that **without** `stream_options: {"include_usage": true}` the Databricks streaming response contains **no usage chunk at all**. Setting `general_settings.always_include_stream_usage: true` restores the usage chunk but still yields no cache fields — so the gap is in response parsing, not in the request or in `stream_options` handling. ## Caching is actually working A streamed request with `cache_control` was sent, then the same corpus was sent non-streaming. The non-streaming call reported `cached_tokens: 13303` on its *first* call — i.e. the preceding streaming request had populated the cache. So streaming requests participate in caching normally; the tokens are simply never surfaced in the usage object. This means reported cost for streamed Databricks traffic is inflated relative to the provider's actual metering. ## Cause In `litellm/llms/databricks/chat/transformation.py`: - **Line 643** (non-streaming) works only incidentally: ```python setattr(model_response, "usage", Usage(**completion_response["usage"])) ``` The provider's whole `usage` dict is splatted into `Usage`, so cache keys survive because they happen to be present — not because they are handled. - **Line 665**, `class DatabricksChatResponseIterator(BaseModelResponseIterator)`, has no equivalent. Grepping the entire `litellm/llms/databricks/` tree returns **zero** matches for `cache_creation`, `cache_read`, or `cached_tokens`, whereas `litellm/llms/anthropic/chat/transformation.py` handles them explicitly. `DatabricksConfig` inherits from `AnthropicConfig` (`class DatabricksConfig(DatabricksBase, OpenAILikeChatConfig, AnthropicConfig)`, line 152), but the streaming response iterator is a separate class that does not inherit Anthropic's usage parsing. ## Expected `DatabricksChatResponseIterator` should extract `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` from streaming chunks and populate `usage.prompt_tokens_details`, matching both the Anthropic provider and the Databricks non-streaming path. ## Impact Spend tracking is wrong for any streaming Databricks request that uses prompt caching — which is every request from an Anthropic-format agent client. Cache-aware pricing (`cache_read_input_token_cost`, `cache_creation_input_token_cost`) is configured on the deployment and applied correctly on the Anthropic provider, but cannot take effect here because the token counts never reach the cost calculator. ## Related Separate bug in the same provider, filed as #36931 — the Databricks request path emits LiteLLM's internal `thinking_blocks` field instead of Databricks' documented `reasoning` content block, breaking multi-turn extended thinking. Independent of this issue.

signal.title: [Bug]: Gemini reasoning/thinking content leaks into output_text for /responses with reasoning.effort=medium|high, breaking strict json_schema
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? Calling `litellm.responses()` for a Gemini model with a strict `json_schema` output format works correctly at `reasoning.effort="low"` (or unset), returning clean, schema-conformant JSON. Raising `reasoning.effort` to `"medium"` or `"high"` breaks this: the model's raw chain-of-thought narrative is returned as the `output_text` / message content instead of the requested JSON, and the `strict: true` json_schema constraint is effectively ignored. Example actual output at `reasoning.effort="high"` (this is the full `output[0].content[0].text`, not a summary): ``` **My Approach to Crafting the JSON Response** Okay, here's how I'm approaching this. The task is straightforward: generate a JSON response that says "hello" and gives a score of 1. It needs to be perfectly formatted JSON and nothing else - no extra text, no markdown, no comments, just valid, parseable... [... continues for 400+ tokens of first-person reasoning narrative, sometimes including its own markdown code fence with a correct JSON example buried in the middle, before or without ever emitting the JSON as the actual final answer ...] ``` This strongly looks like the model's "thinking"/reasoning content is not being kept separate from the final answer content when Gemini is accessed through the Responses API surface (there's no native `litellm/llms/gemini/responses/` provider config - I believe this goes through a chat-completions-style bridge). For comparison, OpenAI's own reasoning models keep reasoning content out of the final message content (tracked only via `usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`) - Gemini's thinking content is not being handled the same way here, and it also appears to override/ignore the requested strict `json_schema` format once reasoning is engaged at higher effort. `reasoning_tokens` in the usage response does increase correctly with effort level (e.g. 0 at low, 225-400+ at medium/high), confirming the model *is* being asked to think more - the bug is specifically that that content ends up in the answer instead of being separated out, and that it overrides the structured-output constraint. Reproduced identically on both **v1.90.0** and **v1.96.0** (six minor versions apart), so this isn't a recent regression - it looks like a long-standing gap in how Gemini's thinking output is handled via the Responses API bridge. ### Steps to Reproduce ```python import litellm schema = { "type": "object", "properties": {"greeting": {"type": "string"}, "score": {"type": "number"}}, "required": ["greeting", "score"], "additionalProperties": False, } for effort in ["low", "medium", "high"]: response = litellm.responses( model="gemini-3.5-flash", instructions="You are a helpful assistant. Respond only with JSON matching the schema.", input=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "input_text", "text": "Say hello and give a score of 1."}]}], max_output_tokens=512, reasoning={"effort": effort}, text={"format": {"type": "json_schema", "name": "smoke_test", "strict": True, "schema": schema}}, api_base="http://localhost:4000", # a real LiteLLM Proxy instance, gemini-3.5-flash mapped to gemini/gemini-3.5-flash api_key="sk-...", ) text = response.output[0].content[0].text print(effort, "-> valid JSON prefix:", text.strip().startswith("{"), "| len:", len(text)) ``` Expected output: ``` low -> valid JSON prefix: True | len: ~40 medium -> valid JSON prefix: True | len: ~40 high -> valid JSON prefix: True | len: ~40 ``` Actual output: ``` low -> valid JSON prefix: True | len: 41 medium -> valid JSON prefix: False | len: 1130 high -> valid JSON prefix: False | len: 1465 ``` ### Relevant log output ```shell N/A - no error is raised; the response is returned successfully with status "completed", just with reasoning prose as the content instead of the requested structured JSON. ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Responses API / Gemini provider ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.96.0 (also reproduced on v1.90.0) ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: fix(model_prices): correct Gemini 2.5 shutdown dates and DeepSeek V4 max output tokens
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Gemini 2.5 GA models carried no shutdown date - `gemini-embedding-001` shutdown date was two years late - DeepSeek V4 max output capped at 8192, not 384K How it solves it: - Adds Google's announced 2026-10-16 shutdown to Gemini 2.5 GA - Corrects `gemini-embedding-001` to Google's 2026-07-14 date - Raises DeepSeek V4 flash/pro max output to 393216 ## User Flow Before: a developer asking DeepSeek V4 for a long answer, and an admin planning migrations off soon-to-be-retired Gemini models, both get told the wrong thing by the gateway 1. They send GET https://litellm-domain/model/info for their `deepseek-v4-flash` and `deepseek-v4-pro` deployments and read back `"max_output_tokens": 8192`, so a client that sizes `max_tokens` from the gateway truncates at 8K where DeepSeek would have allowed 384K 2. They grep the model metadata the gateway ships for the Gemini 2.5 GA models and find no shutdown date at all, so `gemini-2.5-pro`, `gemini-2.5-flash` and `gemini-2.5-flash-lite` look like they have nothing on the calendar, though Google announced October 16, 2026 3. They find `gemini-embedding-001` marked as going away in 2028 instead of July 14, 2026, so the migration off it never gets scheduled and calls start failing without warning After: the same lookups report what each provider actually published 1. The same GET https://litellm-domain/model/info reports `"max_output_tokens": 393216` for both DeepSeek V4 models, so long generations are sized correctly 2. The Gemini 2.5 GA models all carry a 2026-10-16 shutdown date 3. `gemini-embedding-001` carries 2026-07-14, giving the admin a real date to plan against once #26900 starts surfacing it ## Sources Every changed value comes from the provider's own docs, checked on 2026-08-14 - Gemini shutdown dates: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/deprecations lists `gemini-2.5-pro`, `gemini-2.5-flash` and `gemini-2.5-flash-lite` with shutdown date October 16, 2026, and `gemini-embedding-001` with July 14, 2026 - DeepSeek limits: https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing lists `deepseek-v4-flash` and `deepseek-v4-pro` with context length 1M and "MAX OUTPUT: MAXIMUM 384K". 384K is written as 393216, matching how the registry already stores DeepSeek limits in 1024 units (`deepseek/deepseek-v3.2` is 163840) The wider audit turned up nothing else verifiably stale: Anthropic, OpenAI, Bedrock, Mistral, Cohere, xAI and Azure lifecycle tables already match the registry entry for entry, DeepSeek V4 pricing already matches the current per-token rates, and the Bedrock legacy/EOL table has no pending EOL model that is missing a date The upcoming DeepSeek peak/off-peak repricing takes effect 16:00 UTC on August 16, 2026 and is deliberately left out until it is live, since the registry has no peak/off-peak dimension ## Relevant issues Supports #26900 ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [ ] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) Existing registry coverage in `tests/test_litellm/test_model_prices_schema.py` validates these fields against the schema, including the `deprecation_date` pattern, so no new test was added for a data-only change ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Both runs use the same live proxy on http://localhost:4000, started with `LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config litellm/proxy/dev_config.yaml --port 4000`, against a deployment registered with `curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/model/new -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -d '{"model_name": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro", "litellm_params": {"model": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro"}}'` Before, at base commit `423b791ee0`, the gateway told clients DeepSeek V4 tops out at 8K output tokens: ``` $ curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" http://localhost:4000/model/info \ | jq '.data[] | select(.model_name == "deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro") | {model_name, max_input_tokens: .model_info.max_input_tokens, max_output_tokens: .model_info.max_output_tokens}' { "model_name": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro", "max_input_tokens": 1000000, "max_output_tokens": 8192 } ``` After, at commit `b066ed3e31`, the same request reports the 384K ceiling DeepSeek documents: ``` $ curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" http://localhost:4000/model/info \ | jq '.data[] | select(.model_name == "deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro") | {model_name, max_input_tokens: .model_info.max_input_tokens, max_output_tokens: .model_info.max_output_tokens}' { "model_name": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro", "max_input_tokens": 1000000, "max_output_tokens": 393216 } ``` `deprecation_date` has no reader anywhere in the gateway yet, so no route serves it until #26900 lands, and the registry the gateway ships is the surface that work will read: ``` $ jq '{gemini_2_5_pro: ."gemini/gemini-2.5-pro".deprecation_date, gemini_2_5_flash: ."gemini/gemini-2.5-flash".deprecation_date, gemini_2_5_flash_lite: ."gemini/gemini-2.5-flash-lite".deprecation_date, gemini_embedding_001: ."gemini/gemini-embedding-001".deprecation_date}' litellm/model_prices_and_context_window_backup.json { "gemini_2_5_pro": "2026-10-16", "gemini_2_5_flash": "2026-10-16", "gemini_2_5_flash_lite": "2026-10-16", "gemini_embedding_001": "2026-07-14" } ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Only the Gemini API keys changed, not the Vertex mirrors - DeepSeek peak/off-peak pricing lands separately after August 16 Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/65e89f80ad4346f0aec983f06c6aa0d9

signal.title: [Bug]: interactions.create() silently drops response_format when routed via litellm_proxy (Gemini)
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? When `USE_LITELLM_PROXY=true` (or `litellm.use_litellm_proxy=True`) is set process-wide, `litellm.interactions.create()` for a Gemini model silently loses its `response_format` (JSON schema / mime type constraint) with no error or warning, and the model falls back to free-text output. Root cause, traced through the source: 1. `get_llm_provider()` (`litellm/litellm_core_utils/get_llm_provider_logic.py`) checks `LiteLLMProxyChatConfig._should_use_litellm_proxy_by_default()` **first, unconditionally**, before looking at any explicitly-passed `custom_llm_provider`. With `USE_LITELLM_PROXY=true` set, this forces `custom_llm_provider="litellm_proxy"` for *every* litellm call in the process, including `interactions.create()`. 2. `get_provider_interactions_api_config()` (`litellm/interactions/utils.py`) only recognizes `provider == "gemini"`. For `"litellm_proxy"` it returns `None`. 3. Back in `litellm/interactions/main.py`, when `interactions_api_config is None`, the call **silently bridges to `litellm.responses()`** via `LiteLLMResponsesInteractionsHandler` instead of raising or warning. 4. That bridge's request transform, `transform_interactions_request_to_responses_request()` (`litellm/interactions/litellm_responses_transformation/transformation.py`), maps `system_instruction`, `input`, `tools`, and parts of `generation_config` — but has **no handling for `response_format` at all**. It's dropped entirely, silently. Net effect: a caller who explicitly requested strict JSON-schema output via the Interactions API gets back ordinary free-text (Gemini then wraps its answer in a markdown code fence, as it typically does without an explicit JSON constraint), with no exception and no log line indicating the constraint was dropped. This is especially easy to hit by accident: `USE_LITELLM_PROXY` is a reasonable thing to set globally so that `litellm.responses()`/`litellm.completion()` route through a self-hosted LiteLLM Proxy, but doing so silently breaks the Interactions API for the same process. Confirmed present in every version I checked, `1.82.0` through the current latest `1.96.2` (checked wheel/sdist contents directly) — `litellm/llms/litellm_proxy/interactions/` does not exist in any of them, unlike `litellm/llms/litellm_proxy/{chat,responses,image_generation,image_edit,skills}/` which do. ### Steps to Reproduce ```python import os os.environ["USE_LITELLM_PROXY"] = "true" import litellm response = litellm.interactions.create( model="gemini-3.5-flash", system_instruction="Respond only with JSON matching the schema.", input=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Say hello and give a score of 1."}]}], response_format={ "type": "text", "mime_type": "application/json", "schema": { "type": "object", "properties": {"greeting": {"type": "string"}, "score": {"type": "number"}}, "required": ["greeting", "score"], }, }, generation_config={"max_output_tokens": 512}, api_base="http://localhost:4000", # a real LiteLLM Proxy instance api_key="sk-...", # a valid virtual key for that proxy ) ``` Expected: request reaches the proxy's `/interactions`-equivalent handling (or, if unsupported, the fallback should still honor `response_format`), returning clean JSON. Actual: request is silently rerouted to `/responses` with `response_format` dropped; the returned text is unconstrained free text (often markdown-fenced JSON, not raw JSON), and `json.loads()` on it fails intermittently depending on how the model chooses to format its answer. ### Relevant log output ```shell # No warning/error is logged - the drop is completely silent. Confirmed via the local proxy's # access log: with USE_LITELLM_PROXY=true, an interactions.create() call for a Gemini model never # produces a "/interactions" (or equivalent) hit on the proxy - only "/responses" hits appear, # confirming the silent bridge. ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy / Interactions API ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.96.0 (also reproduced on v1.96.2; confirmed present via source inspection back through v1.82.0) ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: feat(guardrails): add payload, applicability and dispatch controls to generic_guardrail_api
signal.text:
## TLDR Problem this solves: - Guardrail sits on the user's critical path, always - Whole transcript re-sent every turn, O(n^2) per session - Base64 images sent to text-only guardrails - Embeddings and audio calls scanned pointlessly - No way to scope a guardrail to some requests - One logging entry per guardrail call, unbounded per session How it solves it: - `fire_and_forget` dispatches the call, request proceeds immediately - `send_images` / `exclude_payload_fields` / `max_messages` / `max_text_chars` trim the payload - `strip_patterns` removes boilerplate before it leaves LiteLLM - `skip_if_system_prompt_matches` skips out-of-scope requests entirely - `run_only_on_call_types` / `skip_call_types` scope by call type - `skip_if_key_alias_in` / `skip_if_team_id_in` scope by authenticated caller - `guardrail_information_scope` records once per session, or never - All default to today's behavior ## User Flow Before: a team running an observe-only guardrail pays for it on every request, and their agent sessions crawl 1. A developer sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with a 40-turn conversation and a screenshot 2. The request holds until the guardrail service answers, adding its full latency to every turn 3. The guardrail service receives the whole transcript again, plus the base64 screenshot it cannot read 4. Their RAG worker sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/embeddings for 500 chunks, and all 500 are shipped to the same guardrail 5. Requests from an internal agent that another system already tracks are shipped too, with no way to exclude them After: the same team turns the guardrail into a passive observer scoped to agent traffic 1. The proxy admin sets `fire_and_forget: true`, `send_images: false`, `max_messages: 4`, `run_only_on_call_types: [acompletion, anthropic_messages, aresponses]` and `skip_if_system_prompt_matches: ["internal-agent-7f3c"]` on the guardrail, then restarts the proxy 2. The developer sends the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions and gets the completion back at the model's own latency, with the guardrail no longer in the wait 3. The guardrail service still receives the turn, now with the last 4 messages and a `"[omitted]"` marker where the screenshot was 4. The RAG worker's POST https://litellm-domain/v1/embeddings calls return as before and reach the guardrail service zero times 5. Requests whose system prompt names the internal agent reach it zero times, request and response alike 6. Their batch worker's key, whose alias the admin listed, reaches the guardrail service zero times, and pasting that alias into a request body does not buy any other key the same exemption 7. A 40-turn session now carries one guardrail entry in its first spend-log row instead of one per turn per hook, so http://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs stops serving rows tens of thousands of lines long 8. Because nothing waits for the answer, that guardrail can no longer block or rewrite anything, and the proxy log says so at startup ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix All runs below are against a live proxy on `localhost:4000` at commit `7fd8587ebd`, backed by a real postgres so the spend-log rows are the real thing, and calling real Bedrock (`us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0` and `amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0`), so every completion, embedding and token count is billed The guardrail endpoint is a 40-line FastAPI app playing the customer's role: it implements `POST /beta/litellm_basic_guardrail_api`, appends every payload it receives to `inspector.jsonl`, and takes its behavior from the headers each guardrail profile forwards (`x-inspector-delay-ms`, `x-inspector-action`). `GET /_count` returns how many payloads it has received, `POST /_reset` clears them. Nothing else is stubbed Guardrail profiles used, all `default_on: false` so each request opts in by name: ```yaml guardrails: - guardrail_name: gg-baseline # today's behavior litellm_params: {guardrail: generic_guardrail_api, mode: [pre_call, post_call], api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8787, default_on: false} - guardrail_name: gg-payload litellm_params: guardrail: generic_guardrail_api mode: [pre_call] api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8787 default_on: false optional_params: {send_images: false, exclude_payload_fields: [request_headers, litellm_version], max_messages: 2, max_text_chars: 40} - guardrail_name: gg-strip litellm_params: {guardrail: generic_guardrail_api, mode: [pre_call], api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8787, default_on: false, strip_patterns: ['<env>[\s\S]*?</env>']} - guardrail_name: gg-skip litellm_params: {guardrail: generic_guardrail_api, mode: [pre_call, post_call], api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8787, default_on: false, skip_if_system_prompt_matches: ["internal-agent-7f3c"]} - guardrail_name: gg-calltype litellm_params: {guardrail: generic_guardrail_api, mode: [pre_call, post_call], api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8787, default_on: false, run_only_on_call_types: [acompletion]} - guardrail_name: gg-fire-and-forget # endpoint sleeps 3s, then answers BLOCKED litellm_params: guardrail: generic_guardrail_api mode: [pre_call, post_call] api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8787 default_on: false fire_and_forget: true headers: {x-inspector-delay-ms: "3000", x-inspector-action: BLOCKED, x-inspector-blocked-reason: inspector says no} - guardrail_name: gg-sync-block # control: identical endpoint, awaited litellm_params: guardrail: generic_guardrail_api mode: [pre_call] api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8787 default_on: false headers: {x-inspector-delay-ms: "3000", x-inspector-action: BLOCKED, x-inspector-blocked-reason: inspector says no} - guardrail_name: gg-scope-session litellm_params: {guardrail: generic_guardrail_api, mode: [pre_call, post_call], api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8787, default_on: false, guardrail_information_scope: per_session} - guardrail_name: gg-scope-off litellm_params: {guardrail: generic_guardrail_api, mode: [pre_call, post_call], api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8787, default_on: false, guardrail_information_scope: "off"} - guardrail_name: gg-skip-alias litellm_params: {guardrail: generic_guardrail_api, mode: [pre_call, post_call], api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8787, default_on: false, skip_if_key_alias_in: ["e2e-batch-worker"]} ``` ### 1. `fire_and_forget`: same guardrail endpoint, awaited vs dispatched ``` $ curl -s -w "
http=%{http_code} time=%{time_total}s
" -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"bedrock-haiku-4-5","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Reply with exactly: fnf demo"}],"guardrails":["gg-sync-block"]}' {"error":{"message":"inspector says no","type":"None","param":"None","code":"400"}} http=400 time=3.038614s $ # same request, "guardrails":["gg-fire-and-forget"] {"id":"chatcmpl-8075aa46-3c09-4c57-9a19-ffe1060b5941","created":1786597125,"model":"bedrock-haiku-4-5","object":"chat.completion","choices":[{"finish_reason":"stop","index":0,"message":{"content":"fnf demo","role":"assistant"}}],"usage":{"completion_tokens":6,"prompt_tokens":14,"total_tokens":20,...}} http=200 time=0.813436s ``` The awaited profile waits 3s and blocks. The dispatched one returns the real Bedrock completion in 0.81s, which is the model's own latency, and the guardrail's BLOCKED verdict is ignored as documented. Both background calls still arrive: `GET /_count` reports 2 records (the request and the end-of-stream response) a moment later With the endpoint pointed at a dead port and `fail_on_error: true`: ``` $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}
' ... "guardrails":["gg-dead-sync"] # awaited 500 $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}
' ... "guardrails":["gg-dead-fnf"] # fire_and_forget 200 $ grep 'fire_and_forget) call failed' litellm.log | tail -1 Generic Guardrail API (gg-dead-fnf, fire_and_forget) call failed. input_type=request litellm_call_id=75340d17-...: Cannot connect to host 127.0.0.1:9 ``` ### 2. Payload field control: the model sees the image, the guardrail does not ``` $ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{ "model":"bedrock-haiku-4-5", "messages":[ {"role":"system","content":"you are a helpful assistant with a long system prompt that must be truncated"}, {"role":"user","content":"turn one question"}, {"role":"assistant","content":"turn one answer"}, {"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"what color is this image and this text is longer than forty characters"}, {"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAEAAAABACAIAAAAlC+aJ..."}}]} ], "guardrails":["gg-payload"]}' {"content":"The image is **blue** - specifically a bright, vibrant royal blue color that fills the entire square.","usage":{"prompt_tokens":59,"completion_tokens":25}} $ jq '.payload' inspector.jsonl { "input_type": "request", "litellm_call_id": "c4616fd5-13d9-4246-b1a1-0a00d2b84616", "model": "bedrock-haiku-4-5", "texts": [ "turn one answer", "what color is this image and this text i" ], "structured_messages": [ {"role": "assistant", "content": "turn one answer"}, {"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": "what color is this image and this text i"}, {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "[omitted]"}} ]} ], "has_images_key": false, "has_request_headers_key": false, "has_litellm_version_key": false } $ grep -c "iVBORw0KGgo" inspector.jsonl # image bytes that reached the guardrail 0 ``` Bedrock answered "blue", so the model got the real image. The guardrail got a marker, the last 2 messages, the last 2 texts truncated to 40 characters, and neither `request_headers` nor `litellm_version`. `input_type` and `litellm_call_id` are still there: they are protected from exclusion `max_messages` bounding `texts` and not only `structured_messages` is the review fix from Greptile: the translation handlers build the flat list from the whole conversation, so windowing one and not the other left payload size proportional to session length. Windowing shifts text positions, so a returned rewrite is now refused rather than applied to the wrong message ### 3. `strip_patterns`: boilerplate gone, structure intact ``` $ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions ... -d '{ "model":"bedrock-haiku-4-5", "messages":[ {"role":"system","content":"you are helpful
<env>CWD=/Users/itay/secret-project
DATE=2026-08-13</env>
answer briefly"}, {"role":"user","content":"<env>CWD=/tmp</env>Reply with exactly: stripped"}], "tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"read_env","description":"reads <env> blocks","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{}}}}], "guardrails":["gg-strip"]}' $ jq '.payload | {texts, structured_messages, tool_description: .tools[0].function.description}' inspector.jsonl { "texts": ["you are helpful

answer briefly", "Reply with exactly: stripped"], "structured_messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "you are helpful

answer briefly"}, {"role": "user", "content": "Reply with exactly: stripped"} ], "tool_description": "reads <env> blocks" } ``` Both `<env>` blocks are gone from the text. Roles, message count and the tool description that also contains `<env>` are untouched, because only string text fields are rewritten ### 4. Request applicability: system prompt decides, pasted user text does not ``` $ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions ... -d '{"model":"bedrock-haiku-4-5","messages":[{"role":"system","content":"you are internal-agent-7f3c, tracked elsewhere"},{"role":"user","content":"Reply with exactly: skipped"}],"guardrails":["gg-skip"]}' {"content":"skipped"} $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8787/_count {"records":0} $ # the same marker pasted in the USER message instead $ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions ... -d '{"model":"bedrock-haiku-4-5","messages":[{"role":"system","content":"you are helpful"},{"role":"user","content":"Reply with exactly: internal-agent-7f3c"}],"guardrails":["gg-skip"]}' {"content":"internal-agent-7f3c"} $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8787/_count {"records":2} $ jq -c '{input_type: .payload.input_type, texts: .payload.texts}' inspector.jsonl {"input_type":"request","texts":["you are helpful","Reply with exactly: internal-agent-7f3c"]} {"input_type":"response","texts":["internal-agent-7f3c"]} ``` The matched request suppresses both sides, so the response is skipped too even though the response payload carries no system prompt. A user pasting the same string gets scanned normally ### 5. Call-type filter on a real embedding call ``` $ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/embeddings -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"bedrock-titan-embed","input":["some rag chunk"],"guardrails":["gg-calltype"]}' {"model":"bedrock-titan-embed","dims":1024,"prompt_tokens":4} $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8787/_count {"records":0} $ # the same embedding call with the unfiltered guardrail $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8787/_count {"records":1} ``` ### 6. All three LLM endpoints, and the allowlist scoping them With `run_only_on_call_types: [acompletion, anthropic_messages, aresponses]`, each endpoint sends its request and response and embeddings send nothing: ``` POST /v1/chat/completions -> {"records":2} POST /v1/messages -> {"records":2} POST /v1/responses -> {"records":2} POST /v1/embeddings -> {"records":0} ``` Narrowing the same guardrail to `[acompletion]` drops `/v1/messages` to `{"records":0}`, since each hook resolves its own call type ### 7. `guardrail_information_scope`, read back from the spend log ``` $ # three turns of one session through a per_call guardrail (gg-baseline) turn 1 request_id=chatcmpl-646449fe-c64c-47ce-b994-5b1f8b8d9914 {"session_id":"e2e-agent-1786646372-percall","guardrail_entries":[{"guardrail_name":"gg-baseline","guardrail_status":"success"},{"guardrail_name":"gg-baseline","guardrail_status":"success"}]} turn 2 request_id=chatcmpl-bbe522f2-cb27-4220-9620-eb1845162cf1 {"session_id":"e2e-agent-1786646372-percall","guardrail_entries":[{"guardrail_name":"gg-baseline","guardrail_status":"success"},{"guardrail_name":"gg-baseline","guardrail_status":"success"}]} turn 3 request_id=chatcmpl-08d478f2-4e74-495f-80c3-383e1bda4754 {"session_id":"e2e-agent-1786646372-percall","guardrail_entries":[{"guardrail_name":"gg-baseline","guardrail_status":"success"},{"guardrail_name":"gg-baseline","guardrail_status":"success"}]} $ # the same three turns through guardrail_information_scope: per_session turn 1 request_id=chatcmpl-c0f5d2b1-0203-44c3-a78a-7ba1369958b2 {"session_id":"e2e-agent-1786646372-persession","guardrail_entries":[{"guardrail_name":"gg-scope-session","guardrail_status":"success"}]} turn 2 request_id=chatcmpl-8d8f6069-4925-4cb9-abb1-e2e471a789d5 {"session_id":"e2e-agent-1786646372-persession","guardrail_entries":[]} turn 3 request_id=chatcmpl-2c04b232-ef2f-4f0b-92fb-17e95785a014 {"session_id":"e2e-agent-1786646372-persession","guardrail_entries":[]} $ # and with guardrail_information_scope: off request_id=chatcmpl-9795ea36-81cc-492d-a856-931d37394f73 {"session_id":"e2e-agent-1786646372-off","guardrail_entries":[]} $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8787/_count # the guardrail still ran on every one of those calls {"records":16} ``` Each row is read back with `GET /spend/logs?request_id=...`. Under `per_call` every turn carries two entries, one per hook, which is what makes a long session's row enormous. Under `per_session` the session's first turn carries one and the rest carry none, while the guardrail still ran on all of them. Blocks and guardrail failures keep recording under every scope, covered in the unit tests ### 8. Identity filter vs the message-based filter ``` $ # two keys created with /key/generate, distinguished only by key_alias $ # 1) the exempt alias, "guardrails":["gg-skip-alias"] http=200 payloads the guardrail received: {"records":0} $ # 2) a different alias, same request http=200 payloads: {"records":2} $ # 3) the non-exempt key putting the exempt alias in its own system message http=200 payloads: {"records":2} $ # 4) the same forgery against the message-based filter, which the caller CAN trigger http=200 payloads: {"records":0} $ grep "caller controls" litellm.log | head -1 Generic Guardrail API (gg-skip): skip_if_system_prompt_matches / skip_if_first_role_in match on the request body, which the caller controls, so a caller that knows the configured value can exempt itself from this guardrail. Use skip_if_key_alias_in / skip_if_team_id_in when the exemption must hold against the caller. ``` Case 4 is the review finding from veria-ai, reproduced: a caller who knows the configured marker can exempt itself from a message-based filter. The filters keyed on authenticated metadata (cases 1 to 3) cannot be talked into an exemption by the request body, and the message-based ones now say so in their field descriptions and at startup Running the whole sweep (48 assertions over the eight sections above, streaming included) against Bedrock: 48 passed, 0 failed ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats (if any) - `fire_and_forget` cannot block or rewrite; init warns - Its telemetry entry shows ~0ms and `action: NONE` - In-flight calls are dropped on proxy shutdown - Shaped text is never written back, only `BLOCKED` still applies - `max_messages` drops the system prompt past the window - Message-based skips are caller-forgeable; identity ones are not - `per_session` dedup is per worker process, not global - `per_session` needs a session id, else behaves as `per_call` ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR
